title: Scalable drift monitoring in medical imaging AI
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical medical imaging has advanced diagnostics but also poses challenges in maintaining long-term reliability as input data change. To address this, we present MMC+, a modular framework for scalable drift monitoring that builds on our CheXstray framework for real-time drift detection using multi-modal data concordance (MMC). MMC+ provides a flexible architecture that enables cost-effective continuous performance monitoring in real-world healthcare settings. The framework’s capabilities include aggregating information from multiple data streams using statistical tests or distance metrics, leveraging foundation model embeddings to remove the need for site-specific encoder training, and quantifying uncertainty to better communicate drift significance. Validated with data from Massachusetts General Hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic, MMC+ effectively detects significant data shifts that correlate with performance changes and indicates when AI systems may deviate from acceptable performance bounds. The code for MMC+ is publicly available (Link: https://github.com/FJDorfner/MedImaging-ModelDriftMonitoring/tree/MMC_plus ), promoting broader adoption of AI solutions in clinical settings. Our framework significantly advances drift detection while promoting transparency and collaboration in clinical AI research.

title: Functional precision genomics identifies transcriptional features of therapeutic response and drug resistance in high-grade gliomas
abstract: High-grade gliomas (HGGs) are aggressive tumors with poor outcomes and limited treatment options. To identify actionable vulnerabilities and predictive biomarkers, we employed a functional precision oncology approach that combines genomic and transcriptomic profiling with drug testing in patient-derived three-dimensional culture models to enable systematic evaluation of potential targeted therapeutic strategies. While most single-agent therapies showed limited efficacy, inhibitors targeting PI3K signaling, epigenetic regulators, and survival pathways demonstrated activity in subsets of cases. Genomic alterations and transcriptional programs provided complementary insight into ex vivo drug response. Mesenchymal gliomas were particularly sensitive to BET inhibition, whereas adaptive PI3K signaling was identified as a candidate resistance mechanism. Rational combination strategies targeting complementary pathways significantly improved therapeutic efficacy across glioma subtypes. The data reveal transcriptional context as a key determinant of therapeutic response in HGG and establish a functional genomics platform to identify biomarkers, resistance mechanisms, and personalized treatment strategies.

title: Cryptography-enabled multi-network emergency communication framework for intelligent healthcare systems
abstract: The progressive digitalisation of healthcare systems, the spread of interconnected medical devices and the expansion of Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) environments are transforming the way clinical information is generated, transmitted and used in emergency situations. In this context, communication reliability, security and continuity play a central role, since delays, infrastructure failures, network congestion or cyberattacks may directly compromise the timeliness of intervention and the clinical outcome. This chapter proposes EMES-H (Emergency Mobile Europe System - Health), a secure multi-network communication framework designed to support, rather than replace, existing emergency infrastructures. The objective of the framework is to enable the protected and continuous transmission of urgent medical information across heterogeneous telecommunication environments by combining cryptographic data protection mechanisms with adaptive network selection and resilient routing strategies. The contribution of the chapter develops along three main lines. First, it examines the role of intelligent healthcare systems, the evolution of IoMT and the communication requirements specific to medical emergencies. Second, it discusses the main security and reliability issues affecting healthcare networks, with particular attention to clinical data protection, operational continuity and the vulnerabilities typical of critical scenarios. Finally, it presents the EMES-H architecture together with its operational workflow, functional modules and principal application scenarios. Overall, EMES-H can be regarded as a modular architecture aimed at strengthening the resilience of emergency healthcare communications. By integrating cryptographic protection, multi-network co-ordination and adaptive transmission logic, the framework provides a coherent basis for the development of safer, more interoperable and more operationally robust intelligent healthcare systems.

title: Latent Correlations Between Longitudinal Systemic Complement Factors and Geographic Atrophy Growth Rate
abstract: Purpose: Investigate associations between square root-transformed (SQRT) geographic atrophy (GA) growth rate and longitudinal systemic complement levels in non-neovascular AMD. Methods: Prospective longitudinal cohort study of patients with GA in the University of Colorado AMD Registry enrolled from August 2014 to September 2022, with ≥1month of follow-up imaging through April 2023. Systemic complement factor level ratios (Bb/Factor B, Ba/Factor B, Factor H, Factor I, C4b/C4, C3a/C3, C3b/C3, sC5b-9/C5) were collected approximately annually. SQRT GA growth rate was quantified on fundus autofluorescence. Correlations between GA growth rate and longitudinal biomarker levels were evaluated using a Bayesian hierarchical joint model. Results: One hundred fifty-five eyes from 88 patients were included. Average SQRT GA growth rate was 0.27mm/year over a mean of 3.3 years and was positively associated with female sex. Ba/Factor B (correlation [credible interval {CrI}]:0.35, 95% CrI: 0.02 to 0.64), and Bb/Factor B (0.20, 95% CrI: -0.086 to 0.48) demonstrated posterior distributions largely above zero, consistent with a positive association. Posterior distributions for Factor I (-0.08, 95% CrI: -0.35 to 0.20) and C3a/C3 (-0.14, 95% CrI: -0.44 to 0.18) were centered below zero, whereas those for Factor H (0.09, 95% CrI: -0.20 to 0.37) and sC5b-9/C5 (0.09, 95% Crl: -0.19 to 0.37) were centered above zero. Conclusions: Systemic alternative pathway biomarkers demonstrated the strongest positive associations with GA growth rate. The pattern of associations in this exploratory analysis supports a hypothesis-generating framework in which differences in alternative pathway regulation may be associated with heterogeneity in GA progression. Future larger studies are needed for external validation of this hypothesis-generating work.

title: Explainable Generative Modeling for IDH Mutation Prediction in Glioma: A Conditional VAE with Counterfactual Synthesis and Interpretability
abstract: Glioma is the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults, and accurate determination of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is important for diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognostic assessment. Currently, definitive IDH status determination relies on molecular analysis of tumor tissue obtained through biopsy or surgical resection, motivating the development of accurate, interpretable, and non-invasive imaging biomarkers. This study proposes an explainable multimodal generative framework for IDH mutation prediction using multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), radiomics, and clinical information. The framework employs a self-supervised 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn imaging representations, a dedicated encoder for radiomic features, and late fusion to construct a unified multimodal representation. A Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) is used for minority-class feature-space augmentation, while a Generalized Additive Model with Interactions (GAMI-Net) provides intrinsically interpretable classification without relying on post hoc explanation methods. Experiments were conducted on 622 patients with diffuse glioma from the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, comprising a training cohort of 380 patients, a validation cohort of 96 patients, and a held-out temporal test cohort of 146 patients. On the temporal test cohort, the proposed framework achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.9519 (95% CI: 0.9158–0.9802), an accuracy of 87.7%, and a macro F1-score of 0.847, with higher discrimination than the evaluated DenseNet169-3D and ConvNeXt imaging-only baselines. Intrinsic explainability analysis identified contributions from imaging, radiomic, and clinical information, while global effect functions revealed nonlinear relationships between model features and predicted IDH mutation probability. External evaluation on an independent UCSD cohort showed lower discrimination (AUC = 0.675, 95% CI: 0.513–0.822), highlighting a substantial cross-institutional generalization gap. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the proposed framework combines strong internal temporal discrimination with intrinsic and generative interpretability, while the external results emphasize the need for further multi-center validation and improved robustness to domain shift before clinical deployment.

title: Automated Medical Image Diagnostics Using Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: In this chapter we explain a quantum classical model, for automated image diagnosis. The hybrid quantum classical model mixes processing with a classical deep learning framework. The main goal of the work is to see whether quantum enhanced models can improve image feature extraction and classification accuracy, in imaging. The model looks at non-autistic brain MRwe images. The model must separate autistic brain MRwe images from non-autistic brain MRwe images. That task requires precision and interpretability. We think the model could help doctors. The proposed work uses PennyLane to simulate circuits. Uses TensorFlow / Keras to build classical neural networks. The quantum part and the classical part can work together. We compare the approach with a classical convolutional neural network. The comparison checks accuracy, computational efficiency and model interpretability. Experimental results show that the hybrid model improves performance metrics. The experimental results suggest that quantum layers add clearer feature representations. We see that the hybrid model gives accuracy and better computational efficiency. In our view the hybrid model offers an advantage, over the classical convolutional neural network. We think the proposed work provides an analysis of convergence behavior, parameter optimization and resource utilization, inside the architecture. we think the findings give insight into the benefits and present limits of quantum-classical systems. we think the findings also show how quantum computing can be added to medical imaging solutions.

title: AI-Enhanced Histopathological Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using ACO-Tuned L2-Regularized ResNet50: Toward Early Detection and Clinical Integration
abstract: The most common form of cancer, which is found in females in society, is breast cancer. The diagnosis of the disease is very complex and hence often results in the mortality of the patient. Healthcare practitioners generally use different types of medical imaging-based reports for the precise and timely detection of the disease. In this work, a custom ResNet50 model is trained using the histopathological image samples of benign and malignant cases. A hybrid optimization approach has been used to improve the model performance by resizing the image to 224 × 224 normalization and handling the class imbalance by augmenting the benign samples. By limiting the augmentation to the training set, data leakage has been prevented. In this work, searching the hyperparameter space and finding the optimal values of batch size, learning rate, and epsilon is treated as one of the most crucial parts for which ant colony optimization (ACO) has been used. During model training, the amount of regularization is adjusted in such a way that it minimizes overfitting and enhances generalization based on the gradient's behavior, which has been introduced in an adaptive L2 ridge regularization scheme. Other than fine-tuning the model, ACO-based optimization and adaptive L2 regularization are performed to enhance the generalization of the model on the histopathological data. The model has shown a promising performance of 98.86% validation accuracy, which has proven the effectiveness of the customizations made to the model during implementation. title: Genetic study of a case of complex neurodevelopmental disorder using whole-exome sequencing combined with optical genome mapping
abstract: The clinical phenotypes of complex neurodevelopmental disorders are highly heterogeneous. Besides single-gene mutations, complex chromosomal structural variations are also an important cause of this type of disease. However, some complex structural variants may remain undetected by conventional genetic testing methods, and the underlying molecular etiology remains unresolved in some patients. This study aimed to integrate multi-platform genetic testing techniques, analyze complex chromosomal structural rearrangements and possible pathogenicity, and provide information support for clinical diagnosis and treatment as well as genetic counseling. Chromosome karyotype analysis and Whole-Exome Sequencing (WES) were conducted respectively for a child with multiple abnormal manifestations such as delayed language and motor development, microcephaly, and single palmar crease in a family, as well as her parents. WES and Optical Genome Mapping (OGM) were performed, and functional annotation and gene interaction mapping analysis were performed on the copy number variation regions obtained from OGM. Based on family validation and database search, the source of the mutation and the genotype-phenotype association were analyzed. Karyotype analysis suggested a possible paracentric inversion involving the 1q24-q43 region of chromosome 1 in the child, while both parents had normal karyotypes. WES did not identify definite pathogenic or likely pathogenic point mutations strongly associated with the patient’s phenotype. However, heterozygous variants in * SYNE1* , * PEX2 *, * COLQ * and * RBBP8 * genes were detected, which were all inherited from phenotypically unaffected parents. In addition, WES copy number analysis suggested a single copy deletion in 1q24.2-q25.1 region. OGM further revealed a deletion of approximately 4.6 Mb on the long arm of chromosome 1 (1q), accompanied by a complex rearrangement involving breakpoint rejoining. This de novo event encompasses multiple genes associated with nervous system development, cellular metabolism, and cellular function. Functional enrichment and interaction network analysis of the deleted genes showed that most of the deleted genes were concentrated in the functional classification of basic life activities such as metabolic regulation, immune-related processes, mRNA metabolism and protein synthesis, with multi-pathway and non-specific functional disorders. This study suggests that in children with complex neurodevelopmental disorders, a single-gene point mutation may not fully explain the clinical manifestations, and complex chromosomal structural abnormalities and CNVs may be the main causes. Integrating WES and OGM enables more accurate identification and interpretation of complex structural abnormalities. This approach improves genetic diagnosis and supports mechanistic studies of rare neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: MALAT1::PLAG1 Fusion in Pleomorphic Adenoma with Mucinous and Squamous Metaplasia: A Diagnostic Pitfall Mimicking Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma (ex Pleomorphic Adenoma)
abstract: PURPOSE: Pleomorphic adenoma (PA), the most common salivary neoplasm, is capable of tremendous histologic diversity. Co-occurrence of squamous and mucinous differentiation in PA is a rare phenomenon generally considered within its histologic spectrum, though previously advocated by some as evidence of mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC) ex PA. Herein, we describe a multi-institutional series of MEC-like PA with squamous differentiation, mucous cells, cystic change, and MALAT1::PLAG1 fusion. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Retrospective multi-institutional review identified 5 PAs with MALAT1::PLAG1 fusion. Histopathologic and immunohistochemical slides were reviewed, as well as demographic, clinical, and molecular findings. RESULTS: Five MALAT1::PLAG1-rearranged PA occurred in the parotid gland of 3 female and 2 male patients (median age: 53 yrs, range: 47-58 yrs). Median tumor dimension was 2.5 cm (range: 1.4-3.4 cm). All tumors demonstrated characteristic histologic features of PA as well as areas of cystic squamous and mucinous differentiation resembling MEC (comprising 25-80% of the tumors). There was no capsular invasion or high-grade features. No canonical MEC driver alterations were identified by NGS. No recurrences were identified during available follow-up in 2 patients. CONCLUSION: Cystic squamous and mucinous differentiation may occur in PA, representing a potential diagnostic pitfall both in small biopsy specimens, where it can be misdiagnosed as MEC, as well as in resection specimens where it should not be interpreted as MEC ex PA. Instead, apparent association of these histologic features with MALAT1::PLAG1 fusion suggests a novel genotype-phenotype correlation in PA. Adjunct molecular testing may be valuable in diagnostically challenging cases.

title: Printed and Scanned: Exposing the Fragility of Single-Image Morphing Attack Detectors under Print-Scan Degradation
abstract: Face morphing attacks, in which the biometric traits of two or more identities are blended into a single face image, pose a severe threat to identity document issuance and automated border control. Consequently, a large body of work has proposed Single-image Morphing Attack Detection (S-MAD) algorithms and benchmarked them on datasets such as SYN-MAD22. However, the majority of these benchmarks operate exclusively in the digital domain, which contrasts with the real-world passport issuance pipeline in some countries, which still requires an applicant-supplied photograph to be printed and subsequently re-scanned before it is embedded in the identity document or fed into an automated verification system. This print-scan step introduces halftoning, resampling, color-space, and sensor noise that are absent from digital pipelines, and may mask the high-frequency artifacts that S-MAD models rely on. In this work, we introduce a print-scan version of the SYN-MAD22 dataset, obtained by printing and re-scanning all bona fide and morphed images at 300 and 600 DPI, and we use it to evaluate eight state-of-the-art S-MAD models trained exclusively on digital data. We additionally repeat the acquisition with a second scanner to assess cross-device robustness. Our results show that detectors that achieve near state-of-the-art performance in the digital domain suffer a more than threefold increase in average equal error rate, with the same qualitative degradation observed across both scanning devices, exposing a critical, previously under-reported gap between digital-benchmark performance and robustness to print-scan degradation.

title: Impact of super resolution deep learning reconstruction with a 1024 matrix on CAD-RADS classification of intermediate coronary stenosis: A bicentric retrospective study
abstract: Introduction Moderate coronary stenosis (CAD-RADS 3) is a diagnostic gray zone in coronary CT angiography (CCTA). We evaluated whether super-resolution deep learning reconstruction (SR-DLR), particularly with a 1024 matrix, modifies CAD-RADS classification and inter-reader agreement. Materials and methods: Thirty-nine CCTA examinations from two centers, each containing at least one 50–69% stenosis identified on the routine normal-resolution deep learning reconstruction (NR-DLR), were reconstructed with NR-DLR and SR-DLR (512 and 1024 matrices). Five experienced readers blindly assigned CAD-RADS categories. Agreement was assessed with Gwet's AC2 and paired reclassification with exact McNemar tests. Subgroup analyses (plaque composition, initial image quality) were exploratory. Results Forty-six lesions were analyzed (19 calcified, 16 mixed, 10 non-calcified, one in-stent). Agreement remained excellent (AC2 0.89 [0.86–0.92], 0.87 [0.83–0.90] and 0.84 [0.81–0.88] for NR-DLR, SR-DLR-512 and SR-DLR-1024). Consensus CAD-RADS 2 rose from 6.5% to 21.7% with SR-DLR-1024 (p = 0.016; 10 lesions downgraded, 2 upgraded), predominantly in lesions with non-calcified components. Per-reader CAD-RADS 2 rates ranged from 13% to 30%, increasing significantly for two of five readers (p = 0.004). Conclusion SR-DLR-1024 modified CAD-RADS classification in about one fifth of intermediate lesions while preserving excellent agreement. Without an invasive reference standard, these reclassifications reflect a change in reader interpretation rather than a proven gain in accuracy.

title: ICMarkingSynthetic: A synthetic image dataset of defective integrated circuit markings generated by physics-informed guidelines
abstract: ICMarkingSynthetic is a synthetic image dataset of defective integrated circuit markings generated by physics-informed guidelines. The guidelines distinguish surface abrasion and deposition from changes to the marking itself, covering scratch, contamination, missing text, smeared text, and combined defects. Images are accompanied by labels and generation provenance. These models are cause-derived image-formation approximations, not first-principles material or optical simulations. This record contains the dataset archive and its companion generator archive. Reproduction instructions and annotation limitations are documented in the archive READMEs. The record metadata are public; access to both archives is restricted. Reviewers and researchers may request access by contacting mdsamiul.hoque@utdallas.edu and describing their intended use. Access requests are reviewed individually. title: Histopathology image classification based on ensembles of highly compact features
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we present a method for extracting highly informative yet compact features from histopathological images, which at the same time enable their classification with high accuracy. These types of concise features are very valuable due to the ever-increasing size of datasets as well as the sheer size of histopathology scans. To meet these requirements, we propose new methods for extracting features from the combinations of inner layers of deep neural networks DenseNet-161 and ResNet-152, as well as DINO derived from vision transformers. This is followed by the construction of the subspaces with the help of the principal, as well as neighborhood component analysis. This method creates new features: PCA/NCA-DenseFeats, PCa/NCA-ResFeats, and PCA/NCA-DINO. We then further improve their performance through domain-trained extraction models. The collected results show that the classification accuracy of these features becomes stable even after several-fold reduction of the dimensionality of the baseline features. This means that there is no need to use long representation vectors, and features even several times shorter can be used for classification with almost no information loss. In addition, we propose the multi-architecture ensemble of classifiers orchestrated by the error-correcting output codes method, which utilizes features extracted from three different domain-finetuned models with different architectures: ViT Small, ResNet-152, and DenseNet-161. The proposed solution allows for an increase in accuracy by up to almost 7pp compared to the baseline. The classification vector consumes only 180 float16 values, which is significantly smaller than many other published methods. This reduces the memory required to store features and enables faster classification of these representations. The proposed method was evaluated on the BreakHis breast cancer dataset (achieving 95.39% at 40X, 92.07% at 100X) and the Kather colorectal cancer dataset (97.1%), demonstrating its generalizability and applicability.

title: Temporal lobe cortical thickness and cognition in paediatric cancer survivors previously treated with chemotherapy
abstract: Long-term neurocognitive outcomes in paediatric cancer survivors treated with chemotherapy remain incompletely characterized, particularly in relation to cortical structure. Prior neuroimaging studies have included limited representation of racial and ethnic minority survivors. We analysed temporal lobe cortical thickness and cognition in paediatric cancer survivors treated with chemotherapy (n = 21; 8-25 years post-chemotherapy; aged 15-34 years) and age-matched controls (n = 21). Cognition was assessed using National Institute of Health (NIH) Toolbox scores. Cortical thickness of nine bilateral temporal regions was derived from T1-weighted 3T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using FreeSurfer. Group differences and brain-cognition associations were analysed using adjusted regression models with false discovery rate correction. Survivors scored lower on crystallized (p < 0.001), fluid (p = 0.013) and total cognition scores (p = 0.001). They showed reduced temporal lobe cortical thickness (2.62 ± 0.13 vs. 2.74 ± 0.11 mm; p = 0.001), with reductions in seven subregions. Greater thickness was associated with better cognitive performance in 10 of 27 associations, most prominently for crystallized cognition. Fully corrected T-score sensitivity analyses showed crystallized cognition remained lower in survivors (p = 0.044). Paediatric cancer survivors previously treated with chemotherapy showed reduced temporal lobe cortical thickness, which was associated with worse crystallized cognition, suggesting a potential structure-function association.

title: Morphological and Metrical Mandibular Analysis for Gender Determination in Western Uttar Pradesh Population, India: A Digital Panoramic Study
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The objective of this study was to evaluate the usefulness of morphological and metrical measurements of the mandible jointly for gender determination using digital orthopantomogram (s) (OPG) in the Western Uttar Pradesh population, India. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 800 OPGs were randomly selected from age matched equal sample of males and females (n = 400 each) who reported to the outpatient department between 20 and 40 years of age. Radiographs meeting the selection criteria were assessed for the morphology of the coronoid process, condylar process, sigmoid notch, and flexure of the mandibular posterior ramus bilaterally. The same radiographs were analyzed for 18 mandibular morphometric measurements. All morphological and metric assessments were performed on digital OPGs using CS Imaging 7.0.3 dental software and ImageJ software. RESULTS: The mean age of subjects was 39.82 years and 39.09 years for males and females, respectively. Among total OPGs, angled condylar and round coronoid morphology were noted maximum on both sides and genders, while round and sloping sigmoid notch morphology were seen maximum in males and females, respectively. Regarding posterior mandibular rami flexure morphology, 48% of male OPGs showed bilateral flexure at the level of the occlusal plane, while 58% of females had either straight or flexed at a different level from the occlusal plane. Morphometric measurements in both genders and sides showed that, except for the angle between the condyle and coronoid process, all other variables had a significant (P < 0.05) difference between the genders. Furthermore, condylar height, followed by bicondylar breadth noted as the best gender predictors based upon functional discriminant analysis. CONCLUSIONS: Radiographic morphological features and morphometric measurements of the mandible together could act as an indispensable tool for gender determination in forensics.

title: Learning Pathology-Sensitive Representations for Unsupervised Retinal OCT Anomaly Detection
abstract: Deep learning approaches for retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT) predominantly rely on predefined disease categories, limiting their ability to detect rare or previously unseen abnormalities. While visual foundation models provide transferable representations, their effectiveness in identifying pathological deviations from normal retinal anatomy remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce an unsupervised framework for retinal OCT anomaly detection and localization that adapts pretrained visual representations to normal retinal anatomy through anatomy-aware reconstruction and contrastive triplet learning guided by synthetic structural perturbations, without requiring disease-specific annotations. We systematically investigate the influence of pretraining strategies, anatomy-aware representation adaptation, and anomaly scoring mechanisms on the detection and localization of unseen retinal abnormalities. Our findings demonstrate that adapting pretrained representations to normal retinal structure improves anomaly sensitivity, while pixel-space reconstruction errors and feature-space deviations provide complementary signals for identifying pathological changes. These findings underscore the importance of anatomy-aware representation learning and offer insights into developing generalizable retinal anomaly detection frameworks beyond predefined disease categories.

title: Distinct clinical presentation and prognosis of chronic beryllium disease versus pulmonary sarcoidosis: a national multicentre case–control study
abstract: Extract Chronic beryllium disease (CBD) is a granulomatous lung disease caused by a cell-mediated immune response to beryllium exposure [1] and can closely mimic pulmonary sarcoidosis leading to misdiagnosis as up to 6% of patients initially diagnosed with sarcoidosis harbour CBD [1–3]. Because the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) is not routinely available, costly, and has limited sensitivity when performed once [4], establishing a clinical suspicion of CBD is essential. Indeed, exposure is often unrecognized by patients and may be difficult to identify, including in occupational settings [5].

title: The applications of artificial intelligence in liver transplantation: A comprehensive scoping review
abstract: Liver transplantation (LT) is a complex surgical intervention, with intricate decision-making and risks at all stages before, during and after the procedure itself. Artificial intelligence (AI) may assist the process but has seen limited use. This scoping review assessed primary articles reporting on clinical AI in LT in MEDLINE and Embase from 2000 to September 2026. 196 articles were identified: focusing on the pre-operative period before transplant (21.9%), organ retrieval (9.7%), intra-operative issues (3.6%), short-term post-operative complications (16.8%), long-term post-operative complications (45.9%) and natural language processing (2.0%). 95.9% had retrospective designs and only 12.8% had direct multi-centre data, with the rest from national registries or single centres. 13.8% of studies externally validated their AI tools. Only one study performed a prospective evaluation of their tool with a randomized controlled trial. Progress towards clinically deployable tools will require harmonised, higher-granularity datasets, consistent reporting, and prospective evaluation within real-world transplant workflows.

title: Sequential diagnosis with language models
abstract: We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.

title: SDBench: Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark
abstract: SDBench is a benchmark for evaluating sequential diagnosis systems in medical settings. This benchmark provides a framework for assessing how AI systems can progressively gather information, formulate hypotheses, and arrive at diagnoses through iterative decision-making processes. The main source repository for SDBench is hosted at https://github.com/microsoft/sdbench with the website at https://microsoft.github.io/sdbench.

abstract: This record holds the evidence behind every table, figure and multimedia appendix of the paper "Deterministic Integrity Gates for Large Language Model-Assisted Clinical Manuscript Preparation: Development and Evaluation Study", the evaluated software (MedSci Skills version 3.8.0) with the code written for this evaluation, and a corrected copy of the evaluated software. It contains the detector test cases and results, the seeded-defect benchmark, the re-execution package, the claim-tracing table, the classified findings, all LLM-reviewer inputs and responses with request metadata, the adjudication protocol and labels, and the reporting assessments. The README gives the commands that re-run the evaluation. Scripts are MIT-licensed; data, tables and documents are CC BY 4.0.

title: Humanity in the loop: Reframing artificial intelligence and the global medical imaging divide
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Access to radiology and nuclear medicine remains profoundly unequal across global health systems. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) face persistent shortages in imaging equipment, specialist workforce, digital infrastructure, maintenance, regulation and sustainable financing. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a mechanism to improve imaging access, but it may also reinforce existing inequities. This narrative review examines the potential for discriminative, generative and agentic AI to reduce or widen inequities in LMIC medical imaging and proposes a sociotechnical governance framework based on the concept of Humanity-in-the-Loop. KEY FINDINGS: Discriminative AI may improve image interpretation, triage, segmentation, quantification and image-quality assessment; generative AI may enhance reporting, education, translation, communication, synthetic data generation and research workflows; and agentic AI may coordinate referrals, scheduling, follow-up, supply logistics and imaging pathways. They may also exacerbate inequity through data colonialism, algorithmic under-performance, dataset shift, infrastructure dependence, commercial lock-in, second-tier automation, liability transfer and unequal participation in AI research and development. CONCLUSION: Human-in-the-loop governance is insufficient for equitable AI implementation in LMIC medical imaging because the assumptions underpinning effective human oversight are often absent in resource-constrained settings. The proposed Humanity-in-the-Loop sociotechnical framework embeds equity, local agency, contextual validity and public benefit throughout the AI lifecycle. The framework comprises six interconnected domains: patient humanity, workforce humanity, community humanity, data humanity, system humanity and global humanity. IMPLICATIONS FOR PRACTICE: Responsible implementation of AI in medical imaging requires governance frameworks that extend beyond algorithm performance to include workforce development, data sovereignty, infrastructure, community priorities, equitable partnerships and sustainable capacity building. Adoption of a Humanity-in-the-Loop approach may help ensure that AI narrows rather than widens the medical imaging divide between high-income countries and LMICs.

title: Electrochemotherapy in large and deep-seated soft tissue sarcomas: a pilot study on tumor control, limb preservation, and symptom relief
abstract: Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a locoregional treatment that combines reversible electroporation with chemotherapy to enhance intracellular drug delivery. Clinical evidence for ECT in large, deep-seated, recurrent, or locally advanced soft tissue tumors remains limited. This pilot study primarily evaluated symptom palliation following bleomycin-based ECT, with objective tumor response and treatment-related toxicity assessed as secondary outcomes. Twenty-five patients with recurrent, locally advanced, or metastatic STS tumors resistant to conventional treatments underwent ECT between 2022 and 2025. Bleomycin (15,000 IU/m²) was administered intravenously, followed by electroporation using variable electrode configurations according to tumor characteristics. The primary outcome was symptom palliation. Secondary outcomes included objective tumor response and treatment-related toxicity, while additional clinical outcomes included quality-of-life changes, limb preservation, local progression-free survival (LPFS), and overall survival (OS). The study population had a median tumor size of 87 mm (range 35–320 mm), and 92% of tumors were ≥ 5 cm. Overall symptom palliation was achieved in 16 of 18 symptomatic patients (88.9%), with pain reduction reported in 12 of 14 patients with severe baseline pain (85.7%) and complete cessation of bleeding and tumor-associated discharge in all eight affected patients. EORTC QLQ-C30 scores improved across all evaluated domains, including Global Health, Physical Function, and Role Function, while Pain and Other Symptoms scores decreased significantly (all P < 0.001). ECT enabled conversion to operability in selected unresectable tumors, and long-term limb preservation was achieved in four of the six patients who were initially considered candidates for amputation. An objective response was observed in 21/25 patients (84.0%, 95% CI: 63.9%–95.5%). After a median follow-up of 13.7 months, the 1-year LPFS and OS rates were 56.0% and 76.0%, respectively. The most frequent adverse events were skin reactions and soft tissue necrosis, which were generally manageable with conservative wound care or outpatient debridement. No serious ECT-related systemic adverse events were reported. ECT was associated with symptom palliation, objective tumor response, and manageable treatment-related toxicity in this pilot cohort. These preliminary findings warrant further evaluation in larger prospective controlled studies. Clinical trial registration number : The clinical trial registration code number was (IRCT20190904044697N8, Registration Date: 2022-10-02).

title: Measure-Based Supervision for Tiny Object Detection in Aerial Imagery
abstract: Detection breaks down on objects a few pixels wide for a structural reason: as box side length shrinks, intersection over union (IoU) degenerates toward an indicator of exact pixel coincidence, so a one-pixel error can rewrite both the label assignment and the regression gradient. We avoid this regime by discarding pairwise box matching altogether. A scene is treated instead as an unnormalized positive measure over object centers, log-scales, and categories, and training minimizes a debiased, uncertainty-aware unbalanced optimal transport divergence between the predicted measure and a Gaussian-smoothed annotation measure. Soft correspondences replace hard assignment, and because the marginals are left free, total confidence mass survives as count supervision. A second training-only signal is drawn from the image itself predicted instances are rendered back to pixels through anisotropic Gaussian footprints, a shared blur kernel, pixel integration, and a capacity limited background, then compared with the observation under a Poisson–Gaussian noise model. Scene priors enter through a clipped log-space gate that caps how far context may suppress appearance evidence, a bound we audit by reporting recall on atypical placements alongside aggregate gains. The method reaches 31.7 AP on the AI-TOD-v2 validation split, including 23.4 AP on 2–8-pixel objects, and 36.8, 37.1, and 31.2 AP on SODA-D, SODA-A, and AI-TOD-R, with 53.6 AP on tiny persons in TinyPerson. Ablations isolate the contribution of each component.

title: Research priorities to move ctDNA assays into clinical decision making in early-stage breast cancer
abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) assays are increasingly utilised in early-stage breast cancer; but evidence for decision-making remains incomplete. The Breast International Group (BIG) and National Clinical Trials Network (NCTN) ctDNA working group identified research priorities to advance these assays toward clinical utility: clinical trial designs proving utility and affordability; validating ctDNA dynamics as surrogate endpoint; standardising assays; and evaluating patient-reported outcomes and equity. Prospective, randomised evidence remains essential before implementation.

title: Impact of daily machine performance check on prediction models for patient‐specific quality assurance of multiple‐target stereotactic radiosurgery
abstract: Abstract Background Single‐isocenter multiple‐target (SIMT) stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) delivered with standard linear accelerators (linacs) achieves high dose conformity through modulated fields with small multi‐leaf collimator (MLC) apertures, making patient‐specific quality assurance (PSQA) a critical component of radiotherapy programs. Complexity metrics are established predictors of PSQA results, while daily quality control checks of linacs represent an additional potential source of predictive information. Purpose To investigate whether integrating machine performance check (MPC) parameters with complexity metrics improves machine learning model prediction of the gamma passing rate (GPR) in SIMT SRS PSQA. Methods A total of 1054 volumetric modulated arcs from 245 consecutive patients treated with SIMT SRS were included. The median total planning target volume was 5.03 cc (range 0.31–119.65 cc) treated with 10MV‐FFF beams in 1 fraction of 20 or 24 Gy, or in 3–5 fractions of 27–32 Gy. PSQA was performed field‐by‐field using an electronic portal imaging device (EPID) with a gamma criterion of 3%/1 mm and a 95% tolerance limit. Eighteen arc‐specific plan complexity metrics (aPCM) and ten MPC features were considered. Feature selection based on hierarchical clustering of the Spearman's rank correlation matrix yielded fourteen features (five aPCM, nine MPC). Data were split chronologically according to the QA session date, with the earliest 80% of arcs used for training and the most recent 20% for testing. Four histogram gradient boosting models were trained to predict the GPR of each arc: model A (aPCM and MPC), model B (aPCM only), model C (MPC only), and model D (MPC predicting the residuals of model B). Model performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE) and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Differences between models A and B were assessed with Cohen's f 2 and a Wilcoxon signed‐rank test on residuals. Model explainability was obtained with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). Results Model A showed the best performance (MAE = 1.7% [1.5, 1.9]; AUC = 0.87 [0.79, 0.93]), closely followed by model B (MAE = 1.8% [1.6, 2.0]; AUC = 0.83 [0.75, 0.89]) and model D (MAE = 1.8% [1.6, 2.0]; AUC = 0.83 [0.76, 0.90]). Model C performed markedly worse, particularly in classification ability (MAE = 2.0% [1.7, 2.2]; AUC = 0.64 [0.58, 0.71]). The incremental effect of adding MPC features was small‐to‐medium but not significant on residuals ( f 2 = 0.13 [0.02, 0.27]; Wilcoxon p = 0.213). SHAP identified aPCM as the primary predictors in models A and B, with median MLC gap showing the highest contribution (average absolute SHAP value = 1.66%). Among MPC features, couch rotation accuracy showed the highest contribution ( = 0.27%), considerably smaller than that of aPCM (group mean = 0.07% vs. 0.48%). Conclusions MPC features did not provide meaningful complementary information for predicting PSQA results of SIMT SRS. Complexity metrics related to MLC aperture characteristics were the dominant predictors, indicating an association between arc complexity and PSQA outcomes in SIMT SRS. To reduce variability in EPID field‐by‐field PSQA results, we recommend controlling the complexity of SIMT SRS arcs.

title: Medical Image Recognition and Classification for Lung Cancer Disease Diagnosis using Deep Learning
abstract: The automated recognition of lung cancer in Computed Tomography (CT) images requires effective variability reduction in the images with maintaining important pulmonary features. In this research proposes a preprocessing, segmentation, and CNN-based model for the classification of lung CT images in three classes. The pipeline applies Gaussian filter for noise reduction, normalization and contrast enhancement of the image inputs and subsequently, thresholding segmentation for isolating the lungs. The segmented CT images are then fed into the convolutional extraction of features, rectified linear unit (ReLU), max pooling and fully connected feature transformation layers. The output of the model comes from the Softmax classification layer which discriminates between normal, benign and malignant classes. Evaluation of the model performance is assessed through class-specific measures of accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score, supported with confusion matrix and technical comparisons. The reported evaluation demonstrates consistent classification performance across all three diagnostic classes, confirming the feasibility of using the entire preprocessing, segmentation, and CNN-based classification process for analyzing lung CT images.

title: Agentic Automation of BT-RADS Scoring Using an End-to-End System for Standardized Glioma Follow-up Assessment
abstract: The Brain Tumor Reporting and Data System (BT-RADS) standardizes posttreatment MRI response assessment in patients with diffuse gliomas but requires complex integration of imaging trends, medication effects, and radiation timing. An end-to-end multiagent large language model and convolutional neural network system for automated BTRADS classification was developed and evaluated. Five hundred nine consecutive posttreatment glioma MRI examinations (March 2017-July 2021) from a single center were retrospectively evaluated. An extractor agent identified clinical variables from notes using gpt-oss (OpenAI, 20-billion parameters). A scorer agent applied BTRADS decision logic integrating these with quantitative volumetrics. System accuracy was compared against initial assessments, using expert annotation as the reference standard. Four hundred ninety-two examinations were evaluable. Overall system accuracy was 76.0% (374/492) versus 57.5% (283/492) for initial assessments, an absolute difference of +18.5 percentage points ( P < .001). Cohen kappa between the system and the reference standard was 0.71. The system achieved high sensitivity in context-dependent categories (BT-1b; 100%; BT-1a, 92.7%; BT-3a, 87.5%) and moderate sensitivity for threshold-dependent categories (BT-3c, 74.8%; BT-2, 69.2%; BT-4, 69.3%; BT-3b, 57.1%). The BT-4 positive predictive value was 92.9%. These results support further evaluation of this system as a clinical decision-support tool, with local open-weight inference preserving data privacy. ©RSNA, 2026

title: A multi-dimensional SWOT-based strategic planning framework for tertiary public hospitals during the 15th Five-Year Plan period
abstract: This study aims to develop and empirically test a multi-dimensional SWOT-based strategic planning framework for tertiary public hospitals during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, using a large tertiary hospital in Shenzhen as a case study to demonstrate its application and provide decision-making support for high-quality public hospital development. Taking a tertiary public hospital in Shenzhen as the research subject, a self-designed semi-structured questionnaire was used to survey 531 hospital staff and external stakeholders. The questionnaire covered the selection assessment of internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats, employed a Likert 5-point scale to evaluate the hospital’s overall performance across 14 dimensions, and collected open-ended planning suggestions. Frequency statistics and cross-analysis were used for SWOT analysis, based on which the strategic plan was constructed. Internal staff ( n = 478, 90.02%) constituted the primary cohort, with external stakeholders ( n = 53, 9.98%) providing complementary validation perspectives a limitation we acknowledge in the discussion. The core internal strengths were service attitude and humanistic care, geographical location, and community health center construction; the main weaknesses were insufficient disciplinary competitiveness, lack of high-level talents, and insufficient competitiveness of employee compensation. The primary external opportunities were national/local policy support and regional economic development, while the foremost threats were competition from surrounding hospitals and cost-control pressure from medical insurance payment reforms. Three-dimensional cross-validation showed that service advantages were consistent with the highest-scoring scale item (service attitude) and high-frequency open-ended suggestions (improving service levels); disciplinary and talent weaknesses were corroborated by the low-scoring scale items (research capability, talent cultivation). Based on this, a strategic planning matrix consisting of four types of strategies (SO, ST, WO, and WT) was formed. By integrating empirical data from multiple stakeholder perspectives, this study expands SWOT analysis from an environmental assessment tool into a prescriptive strategic planning framework. The proposed strategic system can provide scientific and operable pathway references for tertiary public hospitals in formulating their 15th Five-Year Plans. Beyond the Chinese context, the methodological framework and generic strategic archetypes (SO, ST, WO, WT) are adaptable to hospitals in other healthcare systems, provided that local contextual factors are incorporated.

title: TRAM-AI: A Framework for Transparency in Reporting of Medical Imaging Datasets for Artificial Intelligence Development
abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate TRAM-AI, a consensus-based checklist for verifying whether medical imaging datasets described as publicly accessible are functionally usable for AI development. Materials and Methods A modified Delphi study was conducted. A steering committee generated candidate checklist items through a targeted literature review. An international expert panel ( n = 33) rated items on criticality and feasibility across two Delphi rounds. Consensus was defined as ≥ 75% agreement on both dimensions. The checklist was pilot-validated in 10 publicly available datasets. An advisory group of four experts from Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa evaluated cross-regional applicability. Results Of 16 candidate items, 14 were retained in the final checklist; one item was removed because of feasibility concerns, and another was merged with an existing item because of conceptual redundancy. All 14 final items achieved consensus for both criticality and feasibility. The final TRAM-AI checklist comprises 14 items across four domains: Dataset Access and Persistence (3 items), Technical Interoperability (4 items), Metadata and Reproducibility (4 items), and Ethical, Legal, and Maintenance considerations (3 items). In pilot validation, all items were applicable to all 10 datasets, compliance was 90% for trusted repository, de-dentification, and subject-level mapping, 10% for archive validation, and 30% for partition keys. All four advisory group members endorsed the checklist. Conclusion TRAM-AI provides a practical framework for verifying the functional accessibility of medical imaging datasets, complementing existing methodological reporting standards. Further evaluation and broader validation across diverse geographic settings are warranted. ©RSNA, 2026

title: Vaccination in Pregnancy with the Bivalent Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine Elicits Significant Specific IgA, IgG, and Secretory Antibody Titers in Human Milk
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The RSVpreF vaccine, licensed for the prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)-associated lower respiratory tract disease in infants <6 months via maternal immunization, protects infants through transplacental-transferred antibodies. Additional benefits may be conferred via vaccine-induced antibodies in human milk, but milk was not collected in clinical trials. Here, we implemented a longitudinal, observational study to characterize RSV-specific antibodies in milk of lactating individuals who did or did not receive RSVpreF in pregnancy. METHODS: Between September 2023 and February 2025, milk samples were self-collected from 73 vaccinated and 28 unvaccinated consented individuals during the first month postpartum and frozen until assessment by Luminex-based multiplex immunoassays. This study compared milk immunoglobulin G (IgG), immunoglobulin A (IgA), and total secretory antibody titers against RSVpreF and RSV G between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups using linear models adjusted for maternal age, race/ethnicity, infant daycare attendance, and presence of older children in the home. As prespecified in the study's statistical analysis plan, the threshold for significance in this interim analysis was set at <0.0001, after adjustment for the primary multiple endpoints. RESULTS: -adjusted < 0.0001). Antibody titers to RSV G (not a vaccine antigen, therefore indicative of responses from prior RSV infection) were not different between groups. CONCLUSIONS: High vaccine-induced secretory antibodies may be particularly important since secretory antibody is the most durable antibody class in milk and mucosa and therefore most likely to provide ongoing protection for infants.

title: High-Precision RCM Motion for Ophthalmic Robotics via Hierarchical QP Control and Authority-Guided Recovery Planning
abstract: General-purpose manipulators can position ophthalmic instruments under a software Remote Centre of Motion (RCM). However, at some reachable configurations that are nonsingular for the tip task alone, the RCM and tip-tracking objectives conflict and the servo oscillates. We formalise this failure as a constraint-induced task singularity: the RCM-projected tip Jacobian loses rank while the unprojected tip Jacobian stays well conditioned. Thus, the effective tip authority collapses although the target remains reachable. We present a high-precision RCM servo architecture with built-in singularity recovery: for each commanded target, an authority-guided planner selects a well-conditioned arm configuration that reaches it and plans an RCM-consistent route, executed by a fixed hierarchical-QP controller. On a 200-scenario kinematic benchmark, the complete nominal-and-recovery protocol reaches 128/128 near-singular targets and 71/72 near-joint-limit targets (100% and 99%, respectively), with the software-RCM residual below 0.142 mm. On a physical 6-DOF arm it executes across four RCM entry points, with a worst-case kinematically reconstructed RCM residual of 178 μm and a median tip-regulation error of 32μm, within the 200μm control requirement adopted for the ophthalmic task.

title: Deep learning enhancement of portable ultra-low-field brain MRI: systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Retrospectively registered protocol of a systematic review and meta-analysis of deep learning (DL) enhancement of portable ultra-low-field (ULF, ≤0.1 T) brain MRI. The review asks whether DL-enhanced ULF images agree better with same-subject high-field (≥1.5 T) MRI than standard ULF images, and whether DL adds value over non-DL processing that combines several acquisitions. PubMed, Embase and Web of Science were searched without date or language limits. Eligible studies were primary studies of humans of any age with paired native and DL-processed ULF brain images and a same-subject high-field MRI or CT reference. The primary outcome is the within-study difference in Fisher-transformed correlations with high-field measurements (Δz), pooled with three-level random-effects models; segmentation overlap, image similarity, volumetric bias, lesions and safety are synthesised by effect direction (SWiM). Risk of bias is assessed with QUADAS-3 (review-specific guidance) and QUADAS-C, and certainty with GRADE. This registration was made after the review was completed. It reproduces the protocol documents as fixed before each stage (eligibility criteria, extraction codebooks, risk-of-bias guidance and statistical analysis plan), attaches the original files with their SHA-256 hashes, and lists all later amendments.

title: MEDA-PKD: a dynamic, real-time analytics platform for precision care in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
abstract: The use of medical real-world data is constrained by fragmented data infrastructures and the absence of tools integrating longitudinal clinical with molecular data at scale. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most common monogenic cause of kidney failure, exemplifies this gap given its phenotypic complexity and the need for individualized treatment decisions. We present MEDA-PKD (MEdical DAta translation service of Polycystic Kidney Disease), an interactive, near-real-time analytics platform that integrates clinical routine with research data from the German AD(H)PKD Tolvaptan Registry (NCT02497521, DRKS00008910) into a harmonized database ( https://doi.org/10.18716/adpkd_registry ). MEDA-PKD provides automated near-real-time analysis and dynamic visualization, replacing traditional static approaches to clinical cohorts. As of March 2026, MEDA-PKD visualized data from 1735 patients (mean follow-up 796 days). eGFR slope analysis of data from patients initiating tolvaptan therapy (332 patients) demonstrates the platform's capacity to evaluate real-world therapeutic impact in real-time. Other tabs include family history, medication, lifestyle, quality of life and a wide array of lab values (20,894 entries). Besides, MEDA-PKD integrates proteomics data and allows for secure individual patient-level data access. MEDA-PKD represents a paradigm shift by transforming static cohort data into a living, actionable knowledge resource in ADPKD and will serve as a template for other diseases.

title: RDM4Researchers: Research Data Management as Research Design – Lecture 1
abstract: This is the handout of the first lecture of RDM4Researchers: Designing Reproducible Life Science Research Across the Data Lifecycle, a training series on research data management for the life sciences. The series is organised by FAIRlab Cologne, the research data management team of the Institute for Biomedical Informatics (BI-K), in cooperation with the research data managers of CRC 1218, CRC 1403, CRC 1607 and BullNet. It follows a research project from the first plan to publishing and preserving its data, one stage per session. This lecture was given on 20th October 2026 at the University of Cologne. The lecture opens with a case. In 2006, a group at Duke University published a gene expression signature that was claimed to predict which chemotherapy a cancer patient would respond to. It was then used in three clinical trials that opened in 2007 and 2008. Two biostatisticians who tried to reproduce the published analysis spent about 1500 hours working out what had happened. The paper was later retracted, along with several others. Starting from that case, the lecture asks why so many published results cannot be verified, when that is decided, and what researchers can do differently in their next project. It draws on evidence from: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, which completed 50 of 193 planned replications Scans of genomics papers that found gene names turned into dates by spreadsheet software A study in which 70 teams analysed the same neuroimaging dataset and reached different results A study that requested data "available on request" from 1792 papers and received them for 123 An example project with mice, confocal imaging and RNA sequencing is followed through four phases, each with one design decision: Planning: the unit of analysis and the sample table Collection: templates with controlled vocabularies Processing and analysis: read-only raw data and a written record of every step Sharing and publishing: each kind of data in the repository of its field, each deposit with a persistent identifier The handout shows every slide with the spoken text of the lecture beneath it, followed by the sources. It is meant for life scientists, from advanced MSc students to PIs, and needs no prior training in research data management. Unless otherwise indicated, the content is licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party material is credited where it appears, and logos are excluded from the licence.

title: Editorial: Innovative approaches to coastal zone monitoring and geodata management
abstract: Coastal zone monitoring becomes useful when observations can be translated into reliable assessments and timely decisions. The challenge is therefore not simply to acquire more geodata, but to preserve their meaning as they move between measurement, analysis and application. This Research Topic brings together five contributions spanning offshore aquaculture, shoreline evolution, port water-level 5 forecasting, marine hazards and coastal economic modelling. Read together, they highlight a shared question: how can heterogeneous observations support decisions across different spatial scales, timescales and levels of uncertainty?Nidzieko and Hoel extend the role of side-scan sonar from underwater imaging to quantitative 10 monitoring of offshore kelp cultivation. Using image registration and sonar geometry, they reconstruct the spatial structure of a commercial installation and estimate kelp length, from which biomass is inferred. Comparison with in situ measurements supports the approach while also identifying the need for site-specific calibration and improved resolution of farm lines. Its broader significance lies in the possibility of obtaining repeatable, spatially extensive measurements without relying exclusively on 15 labour-intensive sampling. Calibration and survey geometry remain central to translating this promise into routine monitoring.Zorlu and Kusak address a complementary timescale by examining shoreline evolution along the western Mersin coast between 1985 and 2022. They combine Landsat imagery, Google Earth Engine, the Digital Shoreline Analysis System and fuzzy C-means clustering to connect shoreline-change rates 20 with spatial patterns and land-cover context. The coexistence of erosion and accretion underscores why coastal change should not be reduced to a single regional trend. Together, these two studies show that useful geodata products require more than automated feature extraction: observations must be interpreted in relation to acquisition geometry, spatial resolution and the environmental setting.At shorter timescales, Wang et al. combine empirical mode decomposition, particle swarm optimization and a radial basis function neural network to predict port water levels. They evaluate the model using observations from four ports and examine lead times of 6, 12 and 24 hours, reporting favourable performance relative to the compared neural-network approaches. This contribution illustrates how signal decomposition and model optimization can complement each other in 30 operationally relevant prediction tasks. However, skill over the tested records should be distinguished from performance under exceptional conditions; the authors identify additional environmental drivers and longer prediction horizons as directions for development. Taken together, these contributions locate innovation at the interfaces between sensing, modelling and 70 use. They do not offer a single universal coastal monitoring system; instead, they provide complementary methods and expose the conditions needed to connect them responsibly. Progress should be judged not only by finer maps or lower prediction errors, but also by whether evidence remains traceable, uncertainty remains visible and outputs support decisions appropriate to their context. This is the central opportunity for coastal zone monitoring and geodata management.

title: “Room-Aware Transformer for Activities of Daily Living Recognition in Adults With Early-Stage Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Using Ambient Sensors: Development and Evaluation Study” (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Background: Unobtrusive sensor-based recognition of activities of daily living (ADLs) could support assessment of everyday functioning in Early-Stage Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD). However, there are many ways to analyze sensor data and infer ADL performance, and few studies have directly compared analytic methods for sensor-based activity recognition. OBJECTIVE This study evaluated whether room-specific sensor representations improve ADLs recognition relative to long short-term memory networks and a global Transformer under heterogeneous real-world conditions. METHODS Following pilot feasibility testing with two adult volunteers, we evaluated five homes of adults with Early-Stage ADRD, comprising 92,765 minute-level observations across 67 home-days. Ambient sensors captured motion, temperature, luminance, humidity, and door events without cameras or wearables, and reviewed activity logs provided 13 activity labels. The room-aware transformer processed room-specific sensor features through separate projection branches, fused them with temporal features, and applied shared multi-head self-attention. Models were trained separately for each home using 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows representing recent motion and brief actions, intermediate room-transition context, and broader daily-routine context, respectively. Ablation experiments compared the room-aware transformer with a global transformer lacking room-specific projections and a unidirectional stacked LSTM. Performance was evaluated on held-out days using accuracy, micro-AUC-ROC, macro-AUC-ROC, and per-class metrics. RESULTS Across five homes and three temporal windows, the room-aware transformer achieved the highest accuracy in 11 of 15 comparisons, micro-AUC in 14, and macro-AUC in eight, with one macro-AUC tie. Its performance ranged from 0.36 to 0.76 for accuracy, 0.79 to 0.92 for micro-AUC, and 0.61 to 0.85 for macro-AUC. Its advantage over the global transformer supports the contribution of room-specific representation beyond self-attention alone. Performance was generally better in Homes A and B, where caregiver ADLs were incorporated as dyadic contextual features, suggesting that caregiver activity may help disambiguate participant routines. Relative superiority did not consistently indicate strong absolute performance, as accuracy remained low in the sensor-only Homes C and D (0.36-0.50). Performance varied by home, feature availability, and temporal window, with no window uniformly optimal. Sleep/Rest was recognized most consistently (F1-score, 0.69-0.95), whereas several infrequent activities showed moderate-to-high AUC but low F1-scores, indicating that class separability did not consistently translate into reliable classification. CONCLUSIONS Room-aware transformer generally outperformed the global transformer and LSTM, demonstrating the potential value of spatially structured modeling for ADL recognition. Nevertheless, substantial variation across homes, activity classes, and temporal windows underscores the need for model improvement and external validation in larger, more diverse residential settings before clinical deployment.

title: ProtBed: a streamlined web platform for exploratory statistics and predictive modeling in quantitative mass spectrometry
abstract: Mass spectrometry proteomics and metabolomics generate high-dimensional quantitative matrices requiring rigorous statistical and machine learning evaluation, yet existing analytical workflows typically depend on programmatic scripting or remote cloud servers that introduce datagovernance constraints. ProtBed is a client-side web application that executes post-extraction data exploration directly in the browser runtime. The platform integrates deterministic preprocessing, pairwise and omnibus hypothesis testing, six-model cross-validated machine learning, and publication-ready visualization while preserving complete local custody of quantitative abundance matrices and clinical metadata. Empirical validation was conducted across four diverse cohorts totaling 250 clinical specimens. On an untargeted GC-MS urine cohort (𝑛 = 40; 356 metabolites), stratified five-fold cross-validated classifiers discriminated diabetic kidney disease with AUC = 0.90 (89% sensitivity, 82% specificity). In a deep-coverage post-mortem substantia nigra tissue cohort (𝑛 = 30; 9,606 quantified proteins), full-matrix modeling achieved out-of-fold AUC = 0.99 using logistic regression (AUC = 0.96 for linear support vector machines) and prioritized neuroinflammatory mediators including SAA1, CRP, and GFAP. ProtBed further resolved multiclass diagnostic arms in plasma extracellular-vesicle proteomics (𝑛 = 124) and characterized dysregulated lipid classes in Alzheimer's disease plasma (𝑛 = 56). ProtBed is freely accessible at https://protbed.com/ .

title: Supplemental Material for: Longitudinal melanonychia as a presenting sign of nail unit squamous cell carcinoma: A case series and narrative review
abstract: Background: Nail unit squamous cell carcinoma (nSCC) presenting as longitudinal melanonychia is underrecognized, particularly among patients with skin of color (SOC). This review identifies patient, tumor, and human papillomavirus (HPV) characteristics.Summary: A review from peer-reviewed articles plus five institutional cases yielded 59 total cases. The majority (69.6%) were male, with a median age of 53 years. Among those with known Fitzpatrick Skin Type or race, 86.9% had SOC. Fingernails accounted for 87.7% of tumors. Longitudinal melanonychia was the only finding in 23.7% of cases, while hyperkeratosis, onychodystrophy, and verrucous changes were reported in 30.5%, 18.6%, and 15.3% of cases, respectively. Hutchinson sign was present in 86.1% of cases, 98.2% of cases had single-nail involvement, and 44% of measured cases had a band width ≥3mm, features classically associated with nail unit melanoma. Most (81.4%) tumors were in situ at diagnosis. When performed, HPV testing was positive in 76.0% of cases, with high‑risk types (including HPV 16, 56, 58, and 59) predominating (76.9%).Key Messages: nSCC should be considered in the differential of longitudinal melanonychia, especially in patients with SOC over age 40 and a history of HPV infection presenting with lateral nailfold involvement, hyperkeratosis, onychodystrophy, or verrucous changes. nSCC presenting as longitudinal melanonychia may have overlapping features with nail unit melanoma, so biopsy is necessary to establish the diagnosis. Recognizing these findings may reduce diagnostic delay and allow earlier, tissue‑sparing treatment.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Various Transfer Learning-Based Deep Learning Frameworks Using Brain Tumor MRI
abstract: Brain tumors are a critical and challenging health issue worldwide, and they often reduce patient survival if they are not identified at an early stage. This study presents an automatic approach to identify and classify brain tumor magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans using several pre-trained deep learning frameworks and compares their relative performance. Four popular frameworks, namely VGG16, Xception, ResNet50, and MobileNetV1, were fine-tuned with a transfer learning technique on 2870 brain tumor MRI training images to predict four classes (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor). A quantitative comparison among all applied frameworks was performed using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. On the held-out test set, VGG16 achieved the highest accuracy (70.1%), followed by Xception (63.7%), MobileNetV1 (53.3%), and ResNet50 (50.8%). The results indicate that VGG16 and Xception outperform the other two frameworks under the same transfer learning setting, while all models show low recall for the glioma class. The study provides a baseline comparison of pre-trained frameworks for brain tumor MRI classification and outlines directions for future research.

title: Spatial proteomic profiling of cardiac stromal populations and microenvironments in systemic sclerosis-associated primary myocardial involvement
abstract: Abstract Objectives To define cardiac stromal heterogeneity and spatial stromal-immune organization in systemic sclerosis-associated virus-negative myocarditis (SSc-VNM), a manifestation of primary SSc heart involvement. Methods Imaging mass cytometry, a single-cell multiplexed spatial proteomic technology, was applied to endomyocardial biopsies from ten patients with SSc-VNM, seven with VNM associated with other systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (a-VNM) and nine with isolated VNM (i-VNM). Single-cell phenotyping, cellular-neighborhood and spatial-interaction analyses, and correlations with histological fibrosis were performed at patient level. Results Among 82,673 segmented cells, we identified seven fibroblast phenotypes and one CD34 + stromal-cell population. The overall fibroblast/stromal compartment was expanded in SSc-VNM compared with i-VNM (adjusted p = 0.00973). The composition of fibroblasts/stromal cells differed profoundly in SSc-VNM compared with a-VNM and i-VNM, with numerical increases in CD34 + stromal cells and SOX9 + and PI16 high /POSTN high fibroblasts and de-enrichment of FAP high /POSTN high fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. Spatial analysis identified ten cellular neighborhoods and revealed distinct SSc-VNM-associated patterns, including altered stromal-immune interaction networks. These included enriched interactions of CD34 + stromal cells and PI16 high /POSTN high fibroblasts with CD163 high /HLA-DR + macrophages and CD68 + mast cells. PI16 high /POSTN high and PI16 - /POSTN high fibroblasts demonstrated the highest collagen type 1 expression among all stromal cell subsets across all VNM entities and PI16 high /POSTN high fibroblasts were numerically increased in biopsies with ≥10% fibrotic remodeling and were spatially associated with collagen-rich areas. Conclusions Our findings refine current concepts of human fibrotic myocardial remodeling and support therapeutic targeting of specific stromal players such as POSTN high fibroblast subpopulations. Key messages What is already known on this topic Primary SSc heart involvement contributes substantially to disease-related mortality, but its pathophysiology remains largely enigmatic, particularly lacking understanding of cellular interactions and spatial architecture. Single-cell studies have established fibroblast heterogeneity in both human cardiac disease and SSc skin and lung tissues. What this study adds We provide a molecular characterization of cardiac stromal cell subpopulations using protein-based definitions and demonstrate dysregulation of several fibroblast/stromal subsets, with increases in CD34 + stromal cells and SOX9 + and PI16 high /POSTN high fibroblasts and de-enrichment of FAP high /POSTN high fibroblasts in SSc-VNM compared with a-VNM and i-VNM. We identify the SOX9 + fibroblast niche as a distinct microenvironment particularly enriched in immune cells, including monocyte and macrophage subsets. We demonstrate major differences in the spatial cellular interaction networks of cardiac fibroblasts/stromal cells in SSc-VNM compared with a-VNM and i-VNM. We identify PI16 high /POSTN high and PI16 - /POSTN high fibroblasts as the main collagen type 1 producing fibroblast subsets. Consistently, PI16 high /POSTN high fibroblasts were numerically increased in biopsies with ≥10% fibrotic remodeling and were associated with collagen-rich areas. How this study might affect research, practice or policy Our study identifies defined cardiac stromal states and stromal-immune niches as potential candidates for future therapeutic intervention in primary SSc heart involvement.

title: Patient perception of high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
abstract: Introduction: Patients with high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (HR-NMIBC) often experience significant emotional distress related to the ongoing demands of disease management, including treatment-related adverse events, and concerns about disease recurrence or progression. This study assessed real-world emotional, physical, and socioeconomic burden of HR-NMIBC in Canada, and explored sex-specific differences. Methods: A cross-sectional survey collected data from physicians who were selected based on actively managing HR-NMIBC patients and patients with HR-NMIBC in Canada. Data included symptoms at diagnosis, treatment experience, patient-reported outcomes (PROs), and sex-specific differences on treatment. Results: Twenty-one physicians provided chart-review data for 126 HR-NMIBC patients (92 male, 34 female). PRO data were available for 78 patients (seven of whom had corresponding physician records and 71 who were obtained separately through Bladder Cancer Canada). Patients reported a broader range and higher prevalence of symptoms at diagnosis than physicians documented, notably nocturia (32% vs. 7%), bladder pain (13% vs. 1%), and fatigue (27% vs. 5%). Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) was the most common first-line treatment (62%), yet 22% of patients were dissatisfied overall, and 19% found it poorly tolerable. Patients reported significant logistical strain from frequent consultations, as well as emotional distress, including anxiety and depression. Women reported more urinary symptoms (e.g., nocturia: 50% vs. 25%, p=0.0273), and experienced greater employment disruption (24% vs. 10%) and caregiver needs (32 vs. 14 hours/week) than men. Conclusions: HR-NMIBC imposes significant physical, emotional, and socioeconomic burdens, with notable discrepancies between physician and patient perceptions of symptoms and treatment impact. Sex-specific differences highlight the need for tailored patient-centered care strategies.
