title: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence in Lung Transplantation
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI)-based applications become increasingly embedded in daily medical practice, it is important that healthcare institutions and providers become familiar with these tools. The integration of machine learning (ML) and AI into routine healthcare delivery means that future healthcare workers will require training to ensure appropriate application of these models. While most clinicians are familiar with traditional biostatistical approaches to medical research, the rapid development in machine learning models has likely left most practitioners underprepared to understand these new AI-based models. This review highlights fundamental concepts in ML/AI modeling, summarizes research published within lung transplantation, and explores potential areas of future research and development.

title: An open vision-language model for diverse medical applications
abstract: Artificial intelligence has high potential for impact in healthcare applications, but its training and deployment are challenging due to diverse data, a complex spectrum of possible tasks and important privacy needs. High-performing foundation models that enable data-efficient fine-tuning for diverse downstream tasks can meaningfully accelerate development in this domain. We introduce MedGemma, a collection of medical vision-language foundation models based on Gemma 3. MedGemma demonstrates advanced medical understanding and reasoning across images and text and multiple medical imaging domains, exceeding the performance of similarly sized generative models while maintaining the general capabilities of the Gemma base models. For out-of-distribution tasks, MedGemma achieves improvements of 2.6-10% in medical image question answering, 15.5-18.1% in chest X-ray finding classification and 10.8% in agentic evaluations compared with the base models. Our results show that fine-tuning MedGemma can be more effective than fine-tuning the base Gemma 3 model for medical tasks, particularly in the setting of limited training data. We additionally introduce MedSigLIP, a medically tuned vision encoder derived from SigLIP. MedSigLIP powers the visual understanding capabilities of MedGemma and, as an encoder, achieves performance comparable to or better than that of many specialized medical image encoders. Taken together, the MedGemma collection provides a strong foundation of medical image and text capabilities, with the potential to accelerate medical research and the development of downstream applications.

title: Quantitative Chest CT–derived Fibrosis and Vascular Remodeling and Acute Exacerbation Risk in Mild Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
abstract: In mild idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, quantitative CT–derived fibrosis burden and vascular remodeling were associated with acute exacerbation risk, with venous and arterial remodeling mediating fibrosis effects, supporting the value of vascular metrics for risk stratification.

title: The RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm (RSNA-ICA) Dataset
abstract: Intracranial aneurysm rupture is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, yet aneurysm detection remains challenging, particularly for small lesions and on routine non-angiographic imaging examinations. To support the development and evaluation of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms for intracranial aneurysm detection and localization, the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), in collaboration with the American Society of Neuroradiology (ASNR), the Society of Neurointerventional Surgery (SNIS), and the European Society of Neuroradiology (ESNR), curated the RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm (RSNA-ICA) Dataset. Developed for the 2025 RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Detection Challenge, RSNA-ICA is a large, publicly available, expert-annotated dataset comprising 7202 CTA, MRA, and MRI series from 4278 adult patients collected across 21 institutions in 12 countries spanning five continents. The dataset includes 2566 CTA, 2166 MRA, and 2470 MRI series from patients with and without intracranial saccular aneurysms, providing substantial geographic and imaging diversity. Expert annotations indicate both aneurysm presence and location, and 178 series additionally include three-dimensional segmentations of challenge-defined vascular locations. RSNA-ICA was used to develop and evaluate algorithms in the 2025 RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Detection Challenge. Of the 7202 image series, 5041 are publicly available through MIRA, while the remainder were used for challenge public and private test sets. The dataset is freely available to the research community for noncommercial use and provides a comprehensive resource for advancing AI-based aneurysm detection across both angiographic and routine neuroimaging examinations.

title: 164 Feature Extraction and Tabular Foundation Modelling for Clinically Integrated Meningioma Grade Prediction
abstract: Abstract Introduction Accurate differentiation between low-grade (WHO grade 1) and high-grade (WHO grades 2–3) meningiomas is central to surgical planning, adjuvant radiotherapy decisions, and determination of surveillance intervals. Although radiomics-based machine learning approaches report high AUC values, balanced accuracy is frequently under-reported, limiting interpretability in class-imbalanced datasets. Furthermore, models requiring multi-sequence MRI inputs can impede integration into routine neuroradiology workflows. We therefore evaluated a tabular foundation model for binary grade prediction, with specific emphasis on deployability within standard clinical imaging pathways, including a reduced-input model using post-contrast T1-weighted imaging (T1ce) alone. Methods The BraTS 2023 meningioma dataset (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR) with neuroradiologist-reviewed segmentations was analysed (n = 701; 526 low-grade, 175 high-grade). Volumetric, morphological, and radiomic features were extracted from tumour sub-compartments using PyRadiomics, alongside patient age and sex. Low-variance features were removed. TabPFN2.5 was implemented using 5-fold stratified cross-validation with 80:20 train–test splits, and decision thresholds were optimised for balanced accuracy. A second model was trained using T1ce-derived features only to reflect standard surveillance imaging. Performance was assessed using ROC AUC and balanced accuracy. Results The multi-sequence model achieved mean ROC AUC 0.760 ± 0.051 and balanced accuracy 0.705 ± 0.032. The T1ce-only model demonstrated comparable internal performance (BraTS: ROC AUC 0.765; balanced accuracy 0.704). However, performance decreased on an independent clinical cohort (ROC AUC 0.639; balanced accuracy 0.555), indicating domain shift between curated challenge data and real-world imaging heterogeneity. Conclusion TabPFN demonstrates competitive grade discrimination while enabling a streamlined, PACS-compatible workflow using T1ce alone, supporting integration into routine meningioma surveillance and preoperative risk stratification pathways.

title: 115 Assessing and assuring equity for artificial intelligence in neuro-oncology with Fairboard
abstract: Abstract Introduction Equity, the absence of unfair, avoidable or remediable differences among groups, is a WHO policy tenet yet rarely measured in medicine. Neuro-oncology is no exception: its models are driven by population-level data with little attention to distinctive subpopulations. We propose an open-source platform to quantify and improve the equity of statistical models in neuro-oncology and beyond. Methods We developed a web-based, no-code application for benchmarking model equity (including AI) in medical research, leveraging healthcare economics, Bayesian and frequentist statistics, neuroimaging, and machine learning. We demonstrate its utility in an evaluation of 648 adult glioma patients across 20 open-source tumour segmentation models (n = 12,960 segmentations), spanning >6 years of machine learning research. Results Higher mean Dice was strongly associated with lower Gini index, i.e., higher overall performance models conveyed less overall performance inequity (Spearman’s rho = -0.956, all p < 0.0001). However, composite performance-equity league tables showed substantial rank reshuffling relative to performance-only rankings, with half of the models shifting by 4 or more positions, demonstrating that equity assessment often alters model selection. 17/20 models conferred a performance advantage to males; only 3 showed a marginal female advantage. Age effects were tissue-dependent: younger patients achieved better whole-tumour but worse tumour-core and enhancing-tumour segmentation. The largest disparities arose from the WHO 2021 diagnosis (IDH-mutant astrocytoma tumour core Dice 0.59 vs GBM IDH-wildtype 0.91) and extent of resection, where gross total resection (GTR) outperformed subtotal (STR) across all tissue classes (all p < 0.003). Conclusions Our open-source platform, deployable on any device via a web browser, enables any user to interrogate the equitable benefit of models across patient subgroups, positioning neuro-oncology to lead in maximising healthcare equity.

title: A cautionary tale on the cost-effectiveness of collaborative AI in real-world medical applications
abstract: Abstract Federated learning (FL) has gained wide popularity as a collaborative learning paradigm allowing collaborative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in sensitive healthcare applications. Nevertheless, the practical implementation of FL presents technical and organizational challenges, as it generally requires complex communication infrastructures. In this context, consensus-based learning (CBL) may represent a promising alternative for collaborative learning, allowing the combination of local knowledge into a federated decision system, while potentially reducing deployment overhead. Nevertheless, a comprehensive assessment of the viability of consensus-based learning as a cost-effective and sustainable alternative to federated learning has not yet been conducted. In this work we propose an extensive benchmark of the accuracy, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability of a panel of FL and CBL methods in a wide range of collaborative medical data analysis scenarios. The benchmark includes 7 different medical datasets, encompassing 3 machine learning tasks, 8 different data modalities, and multi-centric settings involving 3 to 23 clients. Our results reveal that CBL is a cost-effective and more sustainable alternative to FL. When compared across the panel of medical datasets in the considered benchmark, CBL methods provide equivalent accuracy to the one achieved by FL. Nonetheless, CBL significantly reduces training time and communication cost (resp. 15 fold and 131 fold decrease) ( p -value< 0.05). This study opens a novel perspective on the deployment of collaborative AI in real-world applications, whereas the adoption of cost-effective methods is instrumental to achieve sustainability and democratization of AI by alleviating the need for extensive computational resources.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Neuroradiology: Transforming Diagnosis, Prognostication, and Workflow
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping neuroimaging across the entirety of the clinical workflow, encompassing patient scheduling, scan quality assurance, image acquisition and reconstruction, automated lesion detection, pathological characterization, treatment planning, and outcome prognostication. This review synthesizes contemporary evidence through a workflow-centric framework, with particular emphasis on AI tools that have achieved real-world clinical implementation. Although reported technical performance across these domains is frequently compelling, critical deficiencies persist in external validation, human-AI benchmarking, model calibration, and standardized performance reporting, collectively impeding full clinical integration. Emerging evidence suggests that the role of the neuroradiologist is transitioning toward a collaborative human-AI paradigm, rather than one of displacement.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Invisible Orthodontics: From Digital Impressions to Adaptive Treatment Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital transformation in orthodontics has significantly revolutionized clinical practices over recent decades. Advancements such as intraoral scanners, 3D imaging (including cone‐beam computed tomography, CBCT), and advanced treatment planning software have increased diagnostic accuracy and the ability to design personalized treatments. These technologies have primarily focused on static aspects and still require continuous human oversight. Machine learning algorithms, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and artificial neural networks (ANNs), offer superior performance in tasks such as identifying anatomical landmarks on radiographic images, assessing skeletal maturity, and predicting treatment outcomes. Research has shown that AI in static diagnosis and planning has achieved an accuracy greater than 90%, outperforming traditional methods. Moreover, AI reduces processing time, minimizes operator performance variability, and serves as a supportive tool in digital orthodontic workflows. Despite these advancements, there remains a significant gap in research regarding adaptive AI for treatments involving clear aligners. Most studies focus on static planning, while dynamic aspects, such as real‐time treatment adjustments based on the patient's biological responses or deviations in tooth movement, are less explored. This research gap may arise from factors such as patient biological diversity, a lack of real clinical data, and the need for multi‐center validation. Adaptive AI, based on reinforcement learning and digital twin modeling, has the potential to reduce the average treatment duration by approximately 3 to 4 months and increase patient satisfaction. The aim of this review is to provide a comprehensive examination of AI's role in real‐time management of invisible orthodontic treatments, focusing on clear aligner‐based treatments. This study analyzes AI applications going from digital data processing to integration with supervisory platforms, discussing challenges, limitations, and future perspectives. This review not only summarizes current achievements but also proposes practical solutions to overcome existing barriers and presents adaptive AI as a pivotal tool for the future of orthodontics.

title: White matter–cognition mapping in pediatric cancer survivors: a two-cohort NODDI-Bingham study
abstract: Childhood cancer survivors (CS) treated with chemotherapy frequently experience long-term cognitive impairments, commonly referred to as CRCI. Whether these deficits reflect disrupted white matter microstructure, altered microstructure-cognition relationships, or both remains unclear. Here, we applied the NODDI-Bingham model, which quantifies neurite density (NDI), isotropic free water (ISO), and orientation dispersion along primary (ODIp), secondary (ODIs), and total (ODIt) fiber axes, to characterize biophysically specific white matter microstructure in CS and examine its relationship to cognition. Twenty-one pediatric cancer survivors and 21 age-matched healthy controls (HC) underwent multi-shell diffusion MRI. Voxel-wise NODDI-Bingham analyses were performed within JHU atlas regions. Group differences were tested by ANCOVA, and microstructure-cognition associations were examined with the NIH Toolbox Crystallized, Fluid, and Early Childhood composites using group-specific regressions. Confirmatory analyses were performed in an age-matched subsample of the HCP (n = 679). Notably, CS showed reduced NDI in the corona radiata, cerebral peduncles, and corpus callosum, with elevated ODIt and ODIp in the middle cerebellar peduncle, pathways that subserve processing speed and interhemispheric integration, cognitive domains among the most vulnerable in CRCI. Group-specific regressions revealed qualitatively different microstructure-cognition relationships: HC exhibited mixed positive and negative relationships across four of five metrics (138 clusters spanning approximately 305,000 voxels; peak Cohen's d up to 3.00), whereas CS showed a predominantly uniformly negative pattern (67 clusters across 57,000 voxels), with no positive clusters for ISO, ODIt, ODIp, or ODIs, thus highlighting that reduced dispersion and extracellular free water are linked to better cognitive performance in CS. HCP analyses reproduced the HC pattern across all five metrics at proportionally smaller effect sizes, ruling out sample-size effects. NODDI-Bingham identifies two aspects of chemotherapy-related white matter pathology that standard diffusion metrics cannot resolve. First, pediatric cancer survivors show selective elevation of ODIp and ODIt in the cerebellar peduncles and reduced NDI in the corona radiata and corpus callosum, localizing group-level injury to specific fanning and neurite density signatures. Second, whereas in healthy controls white matter shows mixed positive and negative microstructure-cognition relationships, survivors retain only negative relationships for ODIp and ODIt and a diminished mixed pattern for NDI, such that in the chemotherapy-exposed brain, only reduced neurite density and increased primary-axis fanning relate to cognitive impairment. These findings implicate a biophysically specific restructuring of white matter-cognition relationships as a candidate mechanism for CRCI and support NODDI-Bingham as a targeted biomarker panel for monitoring and intervention trials. Abbreviated summary: Nandi, McKenna et al. apply the NODDI-Bingham diffusion model to pediatric cancer survivors and controls, showing chemotherapy is linked to selective white matter changes and a restructuring of microstructure-cognition relationships. The findings position NODDI-Bingham as a candidate biomarker panel for tracking and treating cancer-related cognitive impairment.

title: Cell‐based polygenic risk scores predict clinical progression and prioritize network‐based therapeutic targets in Alzheimer's disease
abstract: BACKGROUND: Late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits substantial biological heterogeneity. We developed a framework linking cell-type-specific polygenic risk profiles to precision medicine in AD. METHODS: Cell-based polygenic risk scores (cbPRSs) derived from single-nucleus RNA-seq co-expression networks were evaluated in Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Framingham Heart Study (FHS) cohorts. Network hubs were prioritized using a graph-based PageRank algorithm and candidate drugs were validated in human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived astrocytes. RESULTS: Cell-based PRS analysis identified two genetic risk axes independent of network cell-type labels: an apolipoprotein E (APOE)-concentrated axis (Ast-M2/Oli-M45) and an APOE-independent axis (Ast-M10/Oli-M50), which predicted accelerated progression to AD (hazard ratio: 1.25-2.02) and correlated with localized temporal lobe atrophy, reduced glucose metabolism, and global amyloid burden. High-risk status specifically upregulated complement C4a protein expression in postmortem brains. PageRank network analysis identified four candidate drugs targeting the APOE-containing astrocyte network. Experimental treatment with estradiol and levetiracetam significantly reduced APOE and complement C4 gene expression in hiPSC-derived astrocytes. DISCUSSION: By integrating cell-based genetic risk with network-level target prioritization, this framework enables robust patient stratification and experimental target validation.

title: Using Diffusion Tensor Imaging to Diagnose Middle Interhemispheric Variant of Holoprosencephaly
abstract: The middle interhemispheric (MIH) variant of holoprosencephaly, or syntelencephaly, is a rare developmental malformation characterized by incomplete separation of the posterior frontal and parietal lobes across midline1. Unlike classic holoprosencephaly, anterior midline structures are typically preserved2. MIH may mimic corpus callosum dysgenesis, particularly on prenatal or early postnatal imaging, creating a potential diagnostic role for advanced neuroimaging techniques3.

title: Integration of neuroimaging signatures of aging and Alzheimer's with fluid biomarkers
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Machine learning algorithms applied to neuroimaging may aid diagnosis and disease monitoring. This study aimed to derive neuroimaging signatures of brain aging (Spatial Pattern of Atrophy for Recognition-Brain Age [SPARE-BA]) and Alzheimer's disease (SPARE-AD) in a diverse sample and to examine their associations with plasma biomarkers, diagnosis, and disease progression. METHODS: SPARE-BA and SPARE-AD were calculated using T1-images from 1297 participants without dementia. Associations between neuroimaging signatures and plasma biomarkers were assessed with partial correlations. Logistic regression and cox proportional hazard models evaluated diagnostic accuracy and clinical progression. RESULTS: SPARE-AD displayed the strongest association with plasma phosphorylated tau 217, whereas SPARE-BA correlated most strongly with plasma neurofilament light. The combination of neuroimaging signatures with plasma biomarkers achieved the highest diagnostic discriminability and strongest associations with clinical progression. DISCUSSION: Neuroimaging signatures of aging and Alzheimer's disease display distinct associations with plasma biomarkers. Neuroimaging signatures combined with plasma biomarkers may improve the detection and prediction of cognitive impairment.

title: Reliability gated cross-modal attention with shear reparameterized directional reasoning for RGB-thermal salient object detection
abstract: Abstract RGB-Thermal (RGB-T) salient object detection localizes salient regions where appearance cues alone are insufficient, since thermal radiation stays informative under poor illumination. Two limitations persist. Cross-modal attention is applied at a strength fixed in advance, so a momentarily uninformative stream continues to contribute in full, and directional reasoning is confined to the two image axes, because diagonal coverage has required a dense affinity mask of quadratic cost. We present CDRNet, a Confidence and Directional Reasoning Network with dual ResNet-50 encoders. Cross-modal attention is reliability-gated: a coefficient estimated for each modality from spatial entropy and gradient energy scales the transferred context through a gated residual, and the attention scale is derived from the cosine discrepancy between the pooled modality embeddings, so sharpness follows the semantic gap instead of a fixed constant, and balanced inputs recover symmetric fusion. Directional reasoning is shear-reparameterized: a circular shear maps each diagonal onto an axis, so a single axial operator covers four orientations at axial rather than quadratic cost, a per-pixel gate exposes the learned anisotropy, and a weight-shared second stage refines the result without additional parameters. A boundary gated decoder returns edge evidence to the representation through multiplicative modulation under auxiliary supervision, and its cross scale aggregator mixes two dilation rates per branch under context-dependent weights. On VT821, VT1000, and VT5000, CDRNet attains S-measure values of 0.908, 0.949, and 0.918, surpasses 19 recent methods on all metrics, and ablations isolate each contribution.

title: Papaya Leaf Disease Detection Using a Hybrid Optimized Vision Transformer with Attention Mechanisms
abstract: Early and precise identification of papaya leaf diseases plays a crucial role in enhancing crop productivity and minimizing agricultural losses. However, existing approaches face challenges in handling complex leaf textures, irregular lesion distributions, and environmental variability. To address these challenges, this study introduces a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based classification framework combined with a hybrid Falcon-Bowerbird Optimization (FBO) strategy for papaya leaf disease recognition. The proposed pipeline utilizes histogram equalization to enhance image contrast and improve feature visibility. The ViT model employs patch-based self-attention to capture local and global dependencies across leaf regions, supporting discriminative feature learning. The hybrid FBO mechanism integrates Satin Bowerbird Optimization, Falcon Optimization, and AdaBelief to optimize hyperparameters and stabilize convergence during training. Experiments were conducted on the BDPapayaLeaf dataset, which contains five categories: Anthracnose, Bacterial Spot, Curl, Ring Spot, and Healthy leaves. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of 97.83%, outperforming the evaluated machine-learning and deep-learning baselines, including CNN, AlexNet, and MobileNetV3. In addition, Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, and LIME were used to provide qualitative insight into image regions contributing to the model’s predictions. The results demonstrate strong classification performance under the evaluated experimental conditions and indicate the potential of the framework for future AI-assisted precision-agriculture applications, subject to further large-scale field validation.

title: CLINES: Clinical LLM-based Information Extraction and Structuring Agent
abstract: Objective Clinical narratives in electronic health records (EHRs) hold diagnostic, therapeutic and temporal information often missing from structured fields; manual chart review remains the de facto standard but is slow, costly and variable. We aimed to develop and evaluate Clinical LLM‑based Information Extraction and Structuring Agent (CLINES), a pipeline that extracts and normalises clinical concepts from free-text notes into ontology-grounded, auditable, schema-ready data without task-specific fine-tuning.Methods and analysis We developed CLINES, a modular multistep pipeline: semantic chunking of long notes; extraction by reasoning-capable large language models (LLM); attribute assignment (assertion, value+unit); Unified Medical Language System normalisation; explicit and relative date resolution; and aggregation into an i2b2-style schema. Evaluation was conducted without task-specific supervised training on deidentified MIMIC-III, 4CE and CORAL (breast, pancreas) notes. Comparators include rule/lexicon systems, transformer encoders, single-prompt LLM baselines, alongside chain-of-thought LLMs and full-size clinical named entity recognition encoders (BERT-base, GatorTron-base). Outcomes were F1 for entity, assertion, value+unit and date processing, reported with 95% bootstrap CIs and paired-bootstrap, false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected tests. Inter-annotator agreement, hallucination taxonomy, cost and component ablations were also assessed.Results Across all datasets and tasks, CLINES ranked first on every task-dataset combination. F1 ranges were 0.69–0.87 (entity), 0.84–0.93 (assertion), 0.77–0.90 (value+unit) and 0.73–0.79 (date, where gold annotations were available). Gains over the strongest single-prompt LLM were +0.21–0.38; transformer encoders trailed by +0.28–0.68 F1 on entity extraction. Performance remained stable as notes lengthened, while transformer baselines lost recall. Code field gains and most assertion/value comparisons were significant at FDR-adjusted p<0.05 on paired-bootstrap tests; mention-level inter-annotator F1 on a cross-annotated subset was 0.82 (assertion κ=0.85); a seven-class taxonomy on 700 stratified false positives found 54% of apparent false positives to be annotation gaps rather than true hallucinations.Conclusion CLINES translates narrative EHR text into ontology-grounded, auditable, schema-ready data, offering a practical route to scale chart review-like extraction for cohort discovery and real-world evidence. CLINES substantially reduces but does not eliminate the need for manual review: the residual hallucination quantified here means human verification remains necessary for safety-critical use. CLINES is model agnostic—open and closed models can be substituted to meet cost, performance and privacy goals.

title: Domain-associated phenotypic patterns with MACF1 variants
abstract: PURPOSE: While heterozygous de novo missense variants in the microtubule-binding GAR domain of Microtubule-actin cross-linking factor 1 (MACF1) cause Lissencephaly 9 with Complex Brainstem Malformations (LIS9) [MIM 618325], the phenotypic impact of variants outside this domain remains unclear. METHODS: We assembled a cohort of 5 affected individuals from 4 unrelated families with biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants who exhibit partially overlapping yet unique phenotypic traits. A sixth individual with a de novo, heterozygous frameshift variant was additionally identified. Combined with previously reported cases, we analyzed genotype and phenotype data from 22 individuals using Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)-based unsupervised hierarchical clustering. RESULTS: Clustering revealed two distinct phenotypic signatures, suggesting domain-associated effects. Variants outside the GAR domain associate with broader neurodevelopmental phenotypes and craniofacial and skeletal involvement. Enrichment analysis (p < 0.001) using OMIM HPO sets supported these findings. In contrast to the GAR domain's strong correlation with LIS9, biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants were linked to distinct developmental anomalies. CONCLUSION: These results expand the phenotypic spectrum of MACF1-related disorders and provide preliminary evidence for domain-associated MACF1 variant effects. While limited by sample size and lack of functional validation, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and underscore the utility of HPO-based clustering for systematic phenotype comparison as additional cases emerge. Comprehensive genetic and phenotypic assessments are essential for understanding the role of MACF1 in development, informing diagnosis, and guiding future research on cytoskeletal regulation in neurodevelopment.

title: A novel deep learning anomaly detection pipeline for predicting PDAC from DNA methylation data
abstract: Background Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is highly lethal, largely because diagnosis typically occurs at advanced, incurable stages. Early detection via blood-based biomarkers could improve risk stratification. We investigated whether whole-blood DNA methylation patterns can identify individuals at elevated PDAC risk years before clinical diagnosis, using a deep learning-based anomaly detection framework applied to methylation array data from prospective cohorts. Methods Autoencoder models were trained on healthy control samples (N=27,185) from diverse sources available in the EWAS Data Hub and applied to Michaud’s prospective cohorts (blood collected between 1982-89), comprising 393 future PDAC cases stratified by cumulative time-to-diagnosis cutoffs (N=26 ≤ 3 y; N=57 ≤ 5 y; N=89 ≤ 7 y; N=138 ≤ 1 0 y) and 431 controls. Autoencoders were trained on windows of 10,000 consecutive CpGs with reconstruction error (REC) scores quantifying methylation anomalies. Predictive value was evaluated via stratified cross-validation using ROC AUC [95% CIs] and benchmarked against raw β-value-based classifiers. External validation was performed in the Framingham cohort (N=14 cases; N=1,331 controls, recruited between 1971-75). Functional enrichment of REC-flagged CpG regions was assessed using gene-set over-representation analysis against KEGG terms. Results In the prospective cohorts, REC-based classification achieved its highest macro AUC of 0.758 [0.696–0.820] in the ≤ 3-years-to-diagnosis subset, versus 0.547 [0.445-0.649] for the 𝛽 -value benchmark (ΔAUC = 0.221, p = 0.010). External validation yielded an AUC of 0.614 [0.452–0.771]. REC-flagged regions were enriched in PDAC-relevant pathways, including p53 signaling and pancreatic cancer. Conclusion Whole-blood DNA methylation harbours prediagnostic PDAC-associated anomalies that are detectable through deep learning-based reconstruction error modelling but not through conventional β-value analysis.

title: B-084 Comprehensive Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) Implementation and Analytical Verification of BCR-ABL1 p210 Transcript Quantification on the GeneXpert Platform
abstract: Abstract Background The BCR::ABL1 fusion is a critical diagnostic marker in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), and quantitative measurement of BCR::ABL1 transcripts by RT-PCR is essential for therapeutic monitoring. The Xpert® BCR-ABL Ultra (Cepheid) is an automated, cartridge-based system that integrates sample preparation and RT-PCR with fluorescent detection, targeting the predominant p210 transcript. In CLIA-certified laboratories, an Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) is required when quality control (QC) materials are not tested daily with patient specimens. We developed and implemented an IQCP for the Xpert assay in 2022 and repeated the process following installation of a new instrument in 2026. This study presents a comparative analysis of IQCP performance between the two instruments, along with over 36 months of weekly QC monitoring data using commercially available external controls. Methods The Xpert BCR-ABL1 IS panel (MMQCI, C130) that includes reference materials with BCR::ABL1 concentrations of 0%, 0.0032%, 0.01%, 0.1%, 1%, and 10% on the International Scale (IS) was used in this study. For IQCP development and analytical verification, the 0.01% (low positive control) and 1% (high positive control) panel members were tested on eight consecutive daily runs in our new instrument. Expected MR ranges were established using the mean molecular response (MR) value ±2 standard deviations (SD). For ongoing quality control, the 0% (negative), 0.01% (low positive), and 1% (high positive) controls were tested weekly with clinical testing for approximately thirty-six weeks. QC monitoring also included evaluation of significant shifts in control values associated with reagent cartridge lot changes or control material lot variations. Results Eight consecutive daily runs of the positive controls yielded mean minimal residual (MR) values of 4.12 ± 0.16 for the low positive control and 1.83 ± 0.12 for the high positive control. In comparison, the corresponding 2022 values were 4.09 ± 0.29 (low positive) and 1.87 ± 0.20 (high positive), demonstrating minimal variation between the two evaluations. Based on these data, the established mean ± 2 standard deviation (SD) acceptance ranges were 3.80-4.44 (2026) versus 3.51-4.68 (2022) for the low positive control, and 1.59-2.07 (2026) versus 1.48-2.26 (2022) for the high positive control. Ongoing weekly QC monitoring over 36 months of patient testing, encompassing 10 lots of the Xpert assay kit and 5 lots of the Xpert BCR-ABL1 IS panel, demonstrated minimal variability (low positive mean 4.10 ± 0.24; high positive mean 1.86 ± 0.13). Overall, four QC failures were observed; however, all results remained within ± 2 SD of the established means. Minor shifts in positive control values were noted following assay lot changes but did not exceed the predefined mean MR ± 2 SD acceptance criteria Conclusion Our laboratory implemented an IQCP for the Xpert BCR-ABL assay with weekly QC monitoring. Longitudinal QC analysis demonstrates sustained assay performance, minimal variability, and no significant deviations over 36 months of patient testing. Analytical verification of the new GeneXpert instrument using the Xpert® BCR-ABL Ultra demonstrated performance comparable to the previous instrument, with faster turnaround time and reduced hands-on workflow.

title: The application value of artificial intelligence in medical imaging: foundations, progress, and challenges
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming medical imaging, reshaping the field as it does everyday life. As imaging data grow in complexity and clinical workloads continue to rise, AI has become increasingly essential for improving diagnostic efficiency and precision. However, despite these technical advances, the clinical adoption of AI in medical imaging remains fragmented, with limited generalizability, insufficient interpretability, and unclear clinical responsibility. In this review, we critically examine the evolution of AI in medical imaging, with a particular focus on its functional roles across the imaging workflow and its actual contributions to contemporary clinical needs. We systematically analyze current application paradigms, identify methodological and translational bottlenecks, and discuss emerging strategies to improve model robustness, interpretability, and clinical integration. In addition, we identify key barriers to the practical implementation of AI in medical imaging, including challenges related to cross-domain generalizability, data privacy issues and regulatory compliance. By examining these opportunities and challenges, this review aims to guide future research directions and foster deeper interdisciplinary collaboration among AI, clinical medicine, and biomedical engineering.

title: Interobserver variability in the interpretation of Papanicolaou tests using the Hologic Genius Digital Diagnostics System: detailed analysis of cytology verification in a large academic laboratory
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Whole-slide digital imaging technology paired with artificial intelligence is transforming the practice of cervical cancer screening. We aimed to evaluate the performance of the Hologic Genius Digital Diagnostics System (HGDDS) for detection of neoplasia and to investigate interobserver variability among users who have undergone HGDDS training. METHODS: A total of 110 ThinPrep Papanicolaou tests were selected, with original diagnoses that included 47 cases of low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or worse (LSIL+); 4 cases of unsatisfactory findings; and 59 cases negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM), including 23 cases with microorganisms. All cases were reviewed by 16 cytologists or cytopathologists using the HGDDS. Interobserver variability and correlation with original diagnoses were assessed. RESULTS: The HGDDS showed greater than 95% sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and accuracy for LSIL+ disease. The overall misinterpretation rate was 5.5%. In total, 3 cases had poor interpretation (≥7/16 misinterpretations), including a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion case with 2 adenocarcinoma responses, an LSIL response, and 4 unsatisfactory responses, as well as 2 NILM cases interpreted as unsatisfactory by most participants due to borderline cellularity. Of 23 cases with microorganisms, organisms were not present in the 60-image gallery for 4 cases. Sensitivity was highest for Trichomonas (93.8%) but was low for other microorganisms (58.9%-68.8%). CONCLUSIONS: In a large academic cytology laboratory, HGDDS review by trained users demonstrated high concordance with adjudicated diagnoses for detection of LSIL+, supporting its effectiveness for identifying epithelial abnormalities. However, user experience with digital morphology is important. During early implementation, laboratories should monitor discordance and consider temporary dual review, with particular attention to borderline cellularity cases and microorganism detection.

title: TCASIA: an integrative atlas linking alternative splicing landscapes for cancer immunotherapy
abstract: Background Identifying robust predictive biomarkers for immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) remains a challenge. While alternative splicing (AS) shapes tumor immunity, the lack of large-scale, consensus-based datasets constrains the characterization of ICB-specific splicing landscapes. Methods We developed TCASIA (the Cancer Alternative Splicing Immunotherapy Atlas), harmonizing >4000 samples across 29 cohorts. A rigorous “2-out-of-4” multi-algorithm consensus framework (rMATS, MAJIQ, SUPPA2, and SplAdder) with a fuzzy matching strategy was used to establish a high-confidence AS landscape. Results TCASIA provides a robust toolkit linking splicing perturbations with clinical phenotypes (response, survival, and immune infiltration). Using this platform, we recapitulated the established FAS exon 6 skipping mechanism and identified IL7R exon 6 skipping as a functionally supported candidate associated with reduced CD8 + T-cell infiltration and poor survival in melanoma. Conclusions TCASIA provides an analytical atlas for investigating splicing-mediated immune evasion and prioritizing isoform-specific candidates for further functional and clinical validation in the context of ICB treatment.

title: Dual-Foundation-Model Ensemble Predicts Gene Expression in Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer for Patient Outcome Stratification
abstract: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) exhibits significant heterogeneity in clinical outcomes and treatment responses. While gene expression profiling has provided important biological and prognostic insight, transcriptomic assays are not routinely incorporated into standard clinical practice, in part due to cost. AI models have been demonstrated to predict gene expression from H&E-stain whole-slide images (WSIs) potentially offering a scalable approach for gathering transcriptomic information for patient stratification and biomarker discovery. We developed and tested models to predict expression of 857 genes directly from H&E-stained whole-slide images (WSI). The best performing final model was a dual-ensemble combining predictions from models trained on features extracted with different foundation models. The dual-ensemble reached 776/857 predictable genes with an average correlation of 0.43 (cross-validation), 0.45 (holdout) and 0.40 (external Frankfurt cohort). Predicted expression strongly correlates with expression of clinically relevant markers (like NECTIN4). Estimated hazard ratios of predicted expression correlated strongly with those of measured expression and genes associated with overall survival for both predicted and measured expression in both cohorts were identified. AI-predicted basal vs. luminal subtypes were associated with overall survival and aligned with the ground-truth (accuracies > 0.8). Findings demonstrate that gene expressions inferred from routine staining can support biomarker discovery and patient stratification in MIBC.

title: An Explainable Weighted Ensemble Deep Learning Framework for Subject-Independent ADHD Detection Using EEG Signals
abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is one of the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disorders and diagnosis is still largely based on behavioral evaluations which can be subjective and time consuming. Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals are a promising objective source of information for the detection of ADHD, as they reflect the underlying neural activity. In this study, a subject independent weighted ensemble approach is proposed for automated classification of ADHD from raw EEG signals. Six deep learning architectures - EEGNet, DeepConvNet, ShallowConvNet, bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) with attention, convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM), and EEG Transformer were systematically evaluated under identical experimental conditions using a strict subject-independent protocol to eliminate data leakage. The three best-performing convolutional models are fused using validation-accuracy-based weighted fusion to form the proposed ensemble. The experimental results demonstrate that the ensemble obtained 94.84% accuracy, 94.85% F1-score, and 95.57% AUC-ROC, which is better than all individual baseline models. Subject-level soft voting correctly classified 18 of the 19 test children, achieving 94.74% accuracy. The observed improvements were statistically significant (p < 0.01), as confirmed by McNemar's test. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) were used to interpret the ensemble's predictions and enhance the model transparency. Frontal and parietal EEG channels, especially P3, F8 and Fp2, were identified as significant for classification, which is in line with previous studies in the field of ADHD. The results presented indicate that ensemble learning combined with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can provide an accurate, interpretable, and clinically relevant framework for the detection of ADHD based on EEG signals.

title: Smart Birdhouse: A Case Study of IoT Technologies for Environmental Monitoring
abstract: Smart birdhouses, that is, sensor-instrumented nest boxes and feeder stations connected through Internet of Things (IoT) networks, provide a practical platform for continuous, minimally intrusive monitoring of avian activity and nest microclimate. This chapter presents an implementation-oriented conceptual case study of a smart birdhouse system developed for environmental and biodiversity monitoring. The implemented prototype combines entrance-event detection using radio frequency identification (RFID) and infrared break-beam sensing, periodic microclimate monitoring using temperature, humidity, air-pressure, and illumination sensors, and optional event-triggered audio/image acquisition. The system is organized as a layered IoT architecture that includes nest-edge sensing and local fusion, gateway-based communication over constrained wireless links, cloud-side ingestion and device management, and application interfaces for dashboards and scientific analysis. Field-deployment experience is used to discuss practical design decisions related to weather exposure, condensation, unstable connectivity, energy budgeting, sensor placement, data buffering, time synchronization, and maintenance in outdoor environments.

title: Medical superintelligence: foundations and aspirations
abstract: , yet how to define and evaluate this aspiration remains unclear. We discuss how AI technologies can contribute to more effective care, introducing six interdependent dimensions of medical intelligence to frame contributions of AI to healthcare delivery. As AI capabilities and their integration into clinical workflows advance, improving the quality of care will require more than superhuman performance on isolated tasks. It will require systems that harness AI, independently and in collaboration with humans, to surpass today's strongest human-led health systems in integrated medical reasoning across the full arc of care. Realising their value will require understanding how these capabilities complement existing medical intelligence and combining them effectively to improve the quality and accessibility of care.

title: Under-recognition of metabolic syndrome in North West London (2000–2023): a 23-year retrospective analysis
abstract: Introduction Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is a cluster of cardiometabolic risk factors associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Despite the rising prevalence of obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and glucose dysregulation, MetS remains inconsistently recognised and coded within electronic health records (EHRs). We aimed to determine the extent of under-recognition of MetS within North West London (NWL) over a 23-year period.Methods The Discover-NOW London Secure Data Environment dataset was retrospectively analysed between 1 January 2000 and 31 July 2023. Adults aged ≥18 years were identified as having MetS if coded within EHRs or if they met ≥3 of 5 American Heart Association (AHA) 2005 diagnostic criteria. An Extended AHA definition incorporating BMI and HbA1c was also applied to reflect routine clinical practice.Results Among 2 096 480 adults registered in NWL during the study period, 975 individuals (0.04%) had a clinician-coded diagnosis of MetS. In contrast, 594 325 individuals (21.2%) met AHA-defined criteria and 875 993 (31.3%) met Extended AHA-defined criteria. Women, individuals of Black or Black British ethnicity, and those from more deprived areas were under-represented in the coded cohort relative to algorithm-defined cohorts.Conclusion Metabolic syndrome is substantially under-recorded within routine clinical coding in NWL. Recognition of the true prevalence of MetS within healthcare datasets may support improved risk stratification, enable population-level surveillance, and facilitate evaluation of MetS-related morbidity and healthcare utilisation.

title: Agentic AI Systems in Radiology: Design, Applications, Evaluation, and Challenges
abstract: Building agents that perceive and act on their environment with a degree of autonomy has long been a focus of artificial intelligence research. This pursuit has become far more practical with the emergence of large language models (LLMs) capable of using natural language to integrate information, follow instructions, and perform forms of reasoning and planning across a wide range of tasks. With its multimodal data streams and orchestrated workflows spanning multiple systems, radiology is uniquely suited to benefit from agents that can adapt to context and automate complex, repetitive tasks. In radiology, LLMs and their multimodal variants have already demonstrated promising performance for individual tasks such as information extraction and report summarization. However, using LLMs in isolation underutilizes their potential to support complex, multistep workflows where decisions depend on evolving context from multiple information sources. Equipping LLMs with external tools and feedback mechanisms enables them to drive systems that exhibit a spectrum of autonomy, ranging from semiautomated workflows to more adaptive agents capable of managing complex processes. This review article examines the design of LLM-driven agentic systems, explores representative radiology applications, discusses evaluation frameworks, and outlines key challenges, including error cascades, tool-use effectiveness, and integration with health information technology infrastructure.

title: Design of Screening Cardiometabolic Opportunities Using Transformative Echocardiography Artificial Intelligence (SCOUT-Echo-AI)
abstract: BACKGROUND: Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is highly prevalent among individuals with cardiovascular disease, but often remains undiagnosed until advanced sequelae such as fibrotic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma develop. ​​Transthoracic echocardiography routinely captures incidental subcostal views of the liver that are not used clinically. The EchoNet-Liver algorithm uses artificial intelligence (AI) to predict the presence of liver disease based on routine clinical echocardiograms. Prospective evaluation in real-world practice is needed to understand the clinical utility and impact of AI-enabled opportunistic liver disease screening. METHODS: The SCOUT-Echo-AI study is a single-arm, prospective, multicenter, open-label pragmatic interventional trial that will be conducted across six diverse U.S. healthcare systems (Kaiser Permanente Northern California, Stanford Healthcare, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, University of California Los Angeles, Northwestern Medicine, and Massachusetts General Brigham). Routine echocardiograms will be analyzed by the EchoNet-Liver AI algorithm with an estimated enrollment of ∼3,000 patients. Treating clinicians or participants themselves will be notified of potential undiagnosed liver disease with site-specific workflows in place to ensure routine clinical care for definitive case confirmation. Primary outcomes will be SLD and fibrotic liver disease detection rates and positive predictive values within 12 months of AI identification. Pre-specified secondary outcomes will assess diagnostic accuracy against other gold-standard modalities, treatment initiation, time to diagnosis, and impact on other clinical events. Outcomes will be compared against historical usual-care and contemporary below-threshold cohorts. CONCLUSION: SCOUT-Echo-AI is a prospective multicenter study evaluating the real-world impact of AI-enabled opportunistic liver disease screening using routine echocardiography.

title: An Explainable Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification Using U-Net and EfficientNet-B7
abstract: Accurate brain tumor localization and tumor/non-tumor classification from multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remain challenging because standalone segmentation and classification models provide complementary but limited information for comprehensive tumor analysis. To address this limitation, a hybrid deep learning framework integrating U-Net and EfficientNet-B7 is proposed. The framework employs U-Net to generate pixel-level tumor segmentation masks from multimodal MRI sequences (T1, T1ce, T2, and FLAIR), followed by tumor region-of-interest (ROI) extraction for EfficientNet-B7-based tumor/non-tumor classification. The segmentation confidence and classification probability are subsequently combined using a weighted probabilistic fusion strategy, with the fusion weight experimentally determined during model development. Experiments were conducted on the BraTS 2023 dataset using subject-wise partitioning into training, validation, and testing subsets at a ratio of 70%:15%:15%, and the experiments were repeated five times using different random initialization seeds. The proposed framework achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.91 and a Jaccard index of 0.86 for segmentation, while achieving 96.8% accuracy, 95.8% sensitivity, 97.5% specificity, 95.5% F1-score, and 0.97 AUC for classification. Comparative evaluation demonstrated higher overall performance than the evaluated baseline architectures, including U-Net, V-Net, ResNet50, and EfficientNet-B7, with statistical differences assessed using paired t-tests at p < 0.05. The results demonstrate that segmentation-guided ROI extraction combined with deep feature-based classification and weighted probabilistic fusion provides an effective approach for automated brain tumor analysis.

title: Repeat-consistency learning for improving repeatability of brain-age prediction from structural MRI
abstract: Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based brain-age prediction is increasingly used as an imaging-derived marker of brain ageing, but good predictive accuracy does not guarantee stable estimates when the same individual is scanned repeatedly. This study proposes repeat-consistency learning (RCL), a training framework that uses same-subject, same-session repeated MRI acquisitions as paired training information. A compact three-dimensional convolutional neural network was trained using a chronological-age prediction loss together with output-level and latent feature-level consistency losses. An unweighted formulation treated all repeated-scan pairs equally, whereas a disagreement-weighted formulation reduced the influence of pairs with larger predicted-age differences. The framework was evaluated using the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies cross-sectional dataset with subject-level training, validation and held-out test partitions. Both RCL formulations showed numerically lower scan-rescan disagreement and narrower Bland-Altman limits of agreement than prediction-only training, while held-out age-prediction performance remained broadly comparable. The unweighted formulation provided the most favourable overall balance between repeatability and predictive accuracy. RCL also reduced prediction shifts under several controlled noise and affine perturbations, although substantial sensitivity to image blurring remained. These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that repeated MRI acquisitions can be incorporated directly into model training to encourage more stable predictions and latent representations while maintaining broadly comparable chronological-age prediction performance. The observed improvements were modest and were demonstrated in a controlled, single-dataset, within-session setting. Validation in larger, multi-site, multi-scanner and longitudinal datasets is therefore required to determine the broader robustness, generalisability and practical utility of the approach.

title: Imagerie des nodules pulmonaires : approche diagnostique
abstract: The detection of pulmonary nodules has increased considerably with the widespread use of chest-computed tomography and the development of low-dose CT lung cancer screening. The pulmonary nodule represents a major diagnostic challenge, requiring rigorous evaluation in order to distinguish benign from malignant lesions while limiting unnecessary invasive investigations. Analysis relies on precise morphological characterization (density, size, margins), assessment of persistence and growth over time, and integration of the clinical context. The Fleischner Society guidelines and the protocols derived from organized screening programs now form the basis of standardized management. This article provides a detailed review of the radiological criteria, decision-making algorithms, and the role of transthoracic needle biopsy in the management of pulmonary nodules.

title: Lung Nodule Detection and False Positive Reduction Using Multi-View and Background Images
abstract: This paper presents a lung nodule detection and false positive reduction approach based on YOLOv8x, multi-view CT representations, and background slices used as negative samples. Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and early detection is essential to improve patient survival. Although computed tomography (CT) provides detailed three-dimensional information about the lungs, the large number of generated slices increases the complexity of radiological analysis and can contribute to diagnostic errors. To address this challenge, Computer-Aided Detection (CAD) systems have been developed to assist radiologists in identifying suspicious regions. In this work, we combine axial, coronal, and sagittal representations in a single YOLOv8x detection pipeline, use additional LIDC-IDRI annotation clusters with fewer than three radiologist markings as auxiliary positive samples, and introduce nodule-free background slices as negative training samples. Detections are consolidated through intra-view clustering and weighted inter-view fusion. Experiments following the LUNA16 cross-validation protocol show that the proposed strategy improves detection performance while substantially reducing false positives. The axial baseline achieved a Competition Performance Metric (CPM) score of 0.553 with 32.61 candidates per scan, whereas the multi-view configuration with a nominal budget of 20,000 background images achieved a CPM score of 0.863 and reduced the average number of candidates to 9.11 per scan while preserving high sensitivity. These results show that the combined use of multiple anatomical views and background-negative training can substantially reduce spurious candidates in CT-based lung nodule detection.

title: Reproducible synthetic clinical letters for seizure frequency information extraction
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Seizure-frequency information is critical for epilepsy research and clinical decision-making, yet it is often documented in highly variable free-text neurology clinic letters that are difficult to share and annotate at scale. This study focused on adult epilepsy clinic letters from patients aged 18 years or older. We aimed to develop a reproducible and privacy-preserving framework for seizure-frequency information extraction by training models using fully synthetic, task-faithful clinical letters. METHODS: We designed a structured label scheme that captures common linguistic patterns of seizure burden, including explicit rates, numeric ranges, cluster-based descriptions, seizure-free durations, unknown frequency, and explicit no-seizure statements. A high-capacity teacher language model was used to generate NHS-style synthetic epilepsy follow-up letters paired with normalised labels, step-by-step rationales, and evidence spans. We fine-tuned multiple open-weight large language models (4-14B parameters) to extract seizure frequency from full letters using either direct numeric outputs or structured labels, optionally augmented with evidence-grounded explanations. Performance was evaluated on a clinician double-checked held-out set of real clinic letters using both fine-grained and pragmatic frequency groupings. RESULTS: Models trained purely on synthetic letters generalised to real-world letters, and structured label targets consistently outperformed direct numeric regression. With 15,000 synthetic training letters, representative models achieved micro-F1 up to 0.79 (fine-grained) and 0.85 (pragmatic) on the real test set, while a medically oriented 4B model reached 0.79 and 0.86, respectively. Evidence-grounded outputs supported rapid clinical verification and facilitated error analysis. CONCLUSION: Task-specific synthetic clinical letters with structured, evidence-grounded supervision enabled reproducible development of seizure-frequency extractors while reducing reliance on sensitive adult patient text. These findings support this approach for adult epilepsy clinic-letter extraction, but do not establish generalisability to paediatric notes or other clinical domains.

title: A rubric landscape for evaluating clinical reasoning in large language models: what exists, what is missing, and what needs to be combined
abstract: Exam-style accuracy does not establish whether large language models (LLMs) reason well over clinical records. We define clinical reasoning as integrating and updating evidence across time and sources to form, revise and justify a patient's problem representation and a defensible plan. This structured narrative review maps three literatures: medical education assessment instruments, clinical LLM benchmarks published from 2023 onwards, and general-domain methods for evaluating long-form generation. We examine six dimensions: problem representation, temporal synthesis, differential and management reasoning, counterfactual reasoning, calibrated uncertainty, and reasoning faithfulness. Preprints are included and flagged. No single instrument covers all six dimensions. Problem representation and differential or management reasoning are reasonably covered, although reliability varies by instrument and setting. TIMER-Eval targets temporal synthesis, and ER-Reason assesses sequential diagnostic belief updating. Dedicated uncertainty and counterfactual evaluations are emerging, but their applicability to longitudinal free-text reasoning remains limited. Factual completeness is well theorised in general-domain evaluation, with early clinical evidence of important omissions. Faithfulness remains the weakest dimension, with one identified clinical causal-ablation study on multiple-choice questions. Existing tools should be combined through binary rubric items, separate completeness and correctness scores, case-specific importance weighting with non-compensable safety caps, temporal order-consistency checks, and chance-corrected reliability reporting. Further design work is needed for calibrated uncertainty, counterfactual reasoning and faithfulness over longitudinal free-text records. This review provides a design rationale, not a validated instrument.

title: Evaluating Expressed Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Model Outputs: A Viewpoint on a Proposed Assessment Framework (Preprint)
abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical documentation, information synthesis, health communication, and decision-support tasks. Evaluation must address the quality of their outputs in clinically meaningful terms, not only whether a response reaches an expected answer. Endpoint correctness can conceal important failures in problem representation, differential prioritisation, response to new evidence, temporal synthesis, uncertainty, and safety. Existing clinical benchmarks address overlapping aspects of these qualities through physician-authored criteria and task-specific scoring, but organise them in different ways. Medical education offers established approaches to making selected aspects of clinical reasoning observable for assessment. Its instruments were developed for human learners: their validity does not transfer automatically to LLMs, and a generated explanation does not establish how a model produced its answer. We therefore use medical-education assessment traditions as sources of constructs and task-design logic, not as prevalidated scoring tools for model outputs. We propose a provisional seven-domain framework for evaluating expressed clinical reasoning: the clinically defensible organisation, interpretation, and updating of available patient information in a generated response. The domains cover accuracy and grounding, validity and completeness, diagnostic and management reasoning, temporal reasoning, uncertainty and updating, clinical safety, and communication. They are organised into an evidential foundation, an expressed-reasoning core, and clinical guardrails. Proposed five-point behavioural anchors are applied only to relevant domains and components. Case-specific reference criteria permit defensible alternatives, and judgements are made using evidence available at the specified decision point. Prespecified safety-critical breaches are flagged separately and cannot be compensated for by strong scores elsewhere. The framework is intended for offline evaluation, error analysis, and benchmark design. It is not a validated measurement instrument, a measure of internal model reasoning, or evidence of readiness for clinical deployment. We outline priorities for independent content review, feasibility testing, domain-level agreement assessment, and evaluation of automated judging before stronger measurement claims are made.

title: AI-Driven Multimodal Risk Assessment Combining CT Imaging Biomarkers and Frailty Scores for Enhanced Mortality Prediction in Surgery Patients
abstract: BACKGROUND: Automated frailty assessment predicts postoperative mortality, but routinely acquired CT imaging may provide complementary physiologic information. We evaluated whether AI-derived CT biomarkers improve one-year mortality prediction beyond an ICD-based Risk Analysis Index (RAI-ICD). STUDY DESIGN: This retrospective cohort linked abdominopelvic CT scans obtained from 2013-2018 at a tertiary academic center to non-emergent surgery within 6 months. RAI-ICD was integrated with automated CT-derived muscle, adiposity, bone, and aortic calcification biomarkers using an XGBoost binary classification model, which we deemed the Unified Multimodal Model (UMM). The primary outcome was one-year all-cause mortality; discrimination, calibration, and decision-curve net benefit were evaluated. RESULTS: Among 7,672 patients, one-year mortality was 12.3%; 7,638 patients were included in primary mortality models. RAI-ICD alone achieved an AUROC of 0.75 and outperformed every individual imaging biomarker. Adding all imaging biomarkers increased AUROC to 0.79 (ΔAUROC +0.04; P<0.001). UMM calibration (slope 1.00; intercept 0.01; ICI 0.01) exceeded RAI-ICD calibration (slope 0.72; intercept 0.04; ICI 0.03), particularly at higher predicted risk. At the Youden-optimal threshold, UMM PPV was 0.24, NPV 0.96, and number needed to screen was 4.1. UMM provided significantly greater net benefit overall and among Robust, Frail, and Very Frail strata. CONCLUSIONS: Integrating automated CT biomarkers with RAI-ICD improved one-year postoperative mortality prediction, high-risk calibration, and clinical net benefit compared with frailty assessment alone. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Public perspectives on artificial intelligence in healthcare in the USA: a cross-sectional survey
abstract: Objective: To evaluate public perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare in the USA and assess variation in trust, comfort and perceived fairness across demographic groups. Methods and analysis: This cross-sectional survey of US adults was conducted between 21 November and 4 December 2025, via YouGov, a private public opinion research firm, using a non-probability-based online panel. The sample included 500 general population respondents and an oversample of 750 adults aged 60+. Survey weights were applied to approximate the US adult population. Responses were measured using Likert-type or categorical scales and analysed using survey-weighted statistical tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons. Primary outcomes included comfort with healthcare providers using AI, attitudes towards AI-generated second opinions, prior use of AI for healthcare, relative trust in AI versus clinicians for health information, preference for AI chatbots versus providers in explaining care plans and perceived effects of AI on healthcare fairness. Results: Among weighted respondents (n=500), 34.0% reported prior healthcare AI use, which was more common among college graduates than those without a high school diploma (46.5% vs 22.9%). Only 25.4% reported being comfortable or very comfortable with their provider using AI, while 43.0% were uncomfortable and 31.5% were neutral. Regarding information trust, 44.5% trusted AI much less than clinicians; 88.4% reported a provider would better help them understand their care plan than a chatbot. Prior AI use was associated with more favourable attitudes towards laboratory/imaging interpretation and AI-assisted referrals. Differences by political affiliation, insurance, health status and age were not statistically significant after FDR correction. Conclusions: AI implementation appears to be outpacing public trust. Higher educational attainment was the most consistent predictor of favourable attitudes. Notably, one-third of respondents were neutral across outcomes, suggesting public attitudes are potentially modifiable. These findings underscore the need for transparent deployment and targeted trust-building strategies to support equitable AI adoption in healthcare.

title: Energy-efficient GW detection with adaptive expert layers an adaptive expert-driven AI for GW detection
abstract: In this paper we propose an Adaptive Hierarchical Mixture of Experts (HMoE) model for energy-efficient, real-time gravitational-wave (GW) detection. The model organises specialized expert subnetworks that focus on different time–frequency characteristics of the GW strain data, and a lightweight gating network that dynamically selects only the most relevant experts for each input. This dynamic expert selection reduces redundant computation and allows the architecture to balance detection accuracy, latency, and power consumption according to signal complexity. To further improve efficiency, the HMoE framework is combined with model-compression techniques, including pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation, so that most of the inference can be executed with low-precision, low-cost operations while preserving detection performance. The model is trained and evaluated on real LIGO and Virgo datasets from the Gravitational Wave Open Science Center, containing a variety of compact binary coalescence events and realistic non-stationary noise. Compared with convolutional and recurrent neural network baselines, the proposed HMoE achieves higher detection accuracy (98% vs. 85–87%), while reducing average inference latency to 8 ms per sample and average power consumption to about 80 W (versus 130–150 W). These results demonstrate that adaptive expert-driven architectures provide a practical route to sustainable, high-throughput GW detection in power-constrained settings such as remote ground-based observatories, edge devices, and future space-based detectors.

title: From Image Interpretation to Clinical Reasoning: Upstream Physician-Context-Aware Multimodal Learning with Causal Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Opportunistic screening using routinely acquired clinical data offers a scalable approach for identifying high-risk individuals before acute events occur. Although chest X-rays (CXRs) capture latent cardiovascular biomarkers and clinical histories provide complementary patient context, existing medical vision-language models are primarily optimized for radiology interpretation rather than prognostic reasoning. We propose a causal reinforcement learning framework for multimodal clinical reasoning that integrates CXRs and physician-authored clinical histories for opportunistic MACE prediction. The framework introduces (1) a role-decoupled dual-LLM architecture that separates reasoning from risk prediction, (2) a dual-action causal reinforcement learning policy for evidence selection and reasoning optimization, and (3) causal token pruning to learn compact multimodal representations. Evaluated on an internal cohort, an emergency department cohort, and the external MIMIC dataset, the proposed framework consistently outperformed unimodal baselines and state-of-the-art medical vision-language models, achieving AUROCs of 0.720, 0.760, and 0.845, respectively. It also substantially improved reasoning quality, achieving higher GREEN scores and higher expert preference while maintaining robust predictive performance across diverse patient populations.

title: Quantitative assessment of cerebral venous outflow on routine CT angiography in acute ischemic stroke
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop and validate a semi-automated, observer-independent method for quantitative assessment of cerebral venous outflow on routine single-phase CT angiography (CTA) in acute ischemic stroke. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this multicenter retrospective study, patients with anterior circulation large-vessel occlusion who underwent baseline CTA were included. Venous attenuation was quantified in predefined cortical and deep venous structures using centerline-based segmentations and automated extraction of intraluminal Hounsfield units. Quantitative measures were compared with established visual venous outflow scores using Spearman correlation. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses assessed discrimination of visually defined opacification categories. RESULTS: A total of 242 patients were analyzed (median age 75 years; median NIHSS 14.5). Quantitative venous attenuation showed strong correlations with visual venous scores at the segment level for cortical veins (ρ = 0.72-0.77; all p < 0.001). Correlations for deep venous structures were moderate overall but increased substantially in proximal occlusions. Composite quantitative metrics demonstrated moderate correlations with corresponding visual scores (ρ = 0.62-0.64; p < 0.001). ROC analyses showed high discrimination of venous opacification states at the segment level (AUC 0.81-0.95; 95% CI 0.74-0.97). Quantitative attenuation values remained measurable in visually non-opacified segments, indicating additional continuous information beyond ordinal grading. Results were consistent across centers and robust to arterial normalization. CONCLUSION: Quantitative venous attenuation derived from routine CTA enables reproducible, observer-independent assessment of cerebral venous outflow, closely reflecting established visual scoring while providing additional continuous information. This approach represents a scalable imaging biomarker with direct applicability to routine stroke imaging workflows. KEY POINTS: Question Visual assessment of cerebral venous outflow is observer-dependent and limited to ordinal grading. Findings Quantitative venous attenuation derived from routine CT angiography closely reflects established visual venous outflow scores at the segment level. Clinical relevance Quantitative assessment of venous outflow from routine CT angiography is feasible and scalable, with direct applicability to clinical stroke imaging workflows.

title: FORENSIC RECOVERY OF VIDEO EVIDENCE FROM DAHUA DHFS4.1 SURVEILLANCE SYSTEMS AFTER FORMATTING
abstract: Video footage from proprietary surveillance systems is central to criminal investigations, yet its forensic recovery remains poorly supported. Conventional carving fails on Dahua systems because the proprietary DHFS4.1 file system uses frame encapsulation, header-footer validation pairs and embedded checksums. This paper addresses two open questions: how each of the four DHFS4.1 validation levels affects the false discovery rate (FDR) and recovery rate, and how quick formatting and partial bulk zero-fill overwriting differ in their impact on recovery. The technique combines dual-signature frame validation, frame-size and checksum consistency checking, and adaptive time sequencing, extending our earlier pipeline; the principal contribution is the validation-level ablation, the paired comparison against three independent tools, and the partial-overwrite study. All methods were executed on forensic images of eleven Dahua NVR hard drives acquired behind a hardware write blocker, so every comparison is paired within drive. The proposed method achieved a recovery rate (RR) of 88.0%, a temporal accuracy (TA) of 89.0% and a file-level FDR of 4.0%; four-level validation reduced the frame-level FDR 13.5-fold, from 27.0% (single signature) to 2.0%, at the cost of a 3.2-percentage-point drop in RR. The RR advantage over each compared tool was statistically significant (paired-samples t-test, n = 11, p < 0.05) and confirmed by the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Quick formatting still permitted 76% recovery, whereas bulk zero-fill reduced it to 34% and raised the file-level FDR to 41%; a collision analysis shows that this increase stems from payload fragmentation rather than chance signature matches. Within the tested scope, the methodology performs comparably to commercial tools and, because every decision rule is published, is re-implementable and transparent. The findings offer practical guidance for prioritising evidence collection from Dahua surveillance systems.
